This study will be evaluating the tolerability of a novel formulation of Rapamycin. The latest version of this study seeks to do so with a novel, oil-based formulation of the drug. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.tagline: Pharmacokinetics of a Novel Oil-Blend Rapamycin Formulation in Dogs with Cancer
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of a Novel Oil-Blend Rapamycin Formulation in Dogs with Cancer

current_roster.description: Sorafenib is a cancer treatment that has been approved for use in human renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. It has a distinctive inhibitory activity that may be especially valuable at preventing the harmful resistance mechanism known as evasive resistance (the promotion of metastasis despite drug activity against the primary tumor) in numerous cancer types. We have previously reported on the tolerability and hints of clinical activity of Sorafenib in dogs with cancer. This background provides a rationale for the further study of Sorafenib in dogs with cancer. In this study we seek to define an optimal dosing schedule for Sorafenib and will also assess its tolerability in dogs with cancer.
current_roster.name: Sorafenib for the Treatment of Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description: Evaluating the safety and efficacy of rabacfosadine (Tanovea-CA1) when combined with doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide and prednisone (T-CHOP) in dogs with previously untreated spontaneous multicentric lymphoma.
current_roster.name: Efficacy of Rabafosadine, Vincristine, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin and Prednisone (T-CHOP) in Dogs with Untreated Lymphoma.

current_roster.description: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant tumor arising from the secretory epithelium of the walls of the bilateral anal sacs. AGASACA accounts for 17% of perianal tumors and 2% of all canine skin tumors in this species. AGASACA displays aggressive biologic behavior. It is both locally invasive and highly metastatic, with a reported metastatic rate of between 26 and 96%. Metastasis to the regional lymph nodes is frequently reported early in the course of the disease, whilst metastasis to distant sites, such as the lungs, liver, spleen and bone (and other heart, mediastinum, pancreas), is typically observed months to years later. Multiple treatment modalities have been utilized in the management of AGASACA, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, electrochemotherapy, and various combinations thereof. Currently, there is no widely accepted 'standard of care' for canine AGASACA, other than to recommend surgical resection of the primary tumor, and to consider adjuvant therapies. Surgery alone is often inadequate in controlling either local and/or metastatic disease, although a more recent paper suggests that surgical outcomes may differ depending upon the stage of the patient, 11 and the extent of surgery performed. However, with surgery alone, local recurrence has been documented in 20 to 45% of dogs with AGASACA , and metastasis in 26 to 96% of cases. The primary purpose of this study is to evaluate the clinical impact of temozolomide in dogs diagnosed with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA). Temozolomide is a chemotherapy drug used in human oncology to treat brain tumors, malignant melanoma, and more recently several different neuroendocrine tumors. Whilst AGASACA in dogs is not embryologically of neuroendocrine origin, it does share many characteristics with those tumor types, and can also respond to similar medications. The use of temozolomide in dogs has been previously reported for brain tumors, lymphoma, and malignant melanoma. Given that there is not a standard-of-care chemotherapy protocol for AGASACA, the investigators hope that temozolomide will demonstrate significant biologic activity for this tumor type, and become part of this diseases clinical management. All enrolled dogs will ideally receive 4 cycles (1 cycle = 5 days) of temozolomide, administered by mouth, at home, on study days 0/1 through 5, days 28 through 32, days 56 through 60, and days 84 through 88 (i.e. 1 cycle every month). Hospital visits will be scheduled immediately prior to each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 0/1, 28, 56, and 84. Appropriate chemotherapy recheck visits will also be scheduled for monitoring purposes 1 week after each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 12, 39, 67, and 95. A final study recheck will be scheduled on study day 112. Blood samples,+/- urine samples, will be collected at most of these recheck visits. Re-staging imaging, including thoracic radiographs (chest x-rays) and abdominal ultrasound, will be undertaken on study days 56 and 112. Participation in this study will cease at day 112.
current_roster.name: Biologic activity and safety of temozolomide in dogs with naturally-occurring apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma: a pilot stud

current_roster.description: Background Insulinoma, the most common pancreatic tumor in dogs, can cause potentially life-threatening hypoglycemia (low glucose). Insulinoma also aggressively metastasizes (spreads to other parts of the body), frequently to the liver and lymph nodes. Treatment of both primary and metastatic disease is essential for improving prognosis. Current treatment options for canine insulinoma are limited and may not provide long-term disease control. Novel treatment approaches are needed to improve long-term outcomes for dogs with this disease. High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that precisely destroys tumor cells while sparing normal organs. H-FIRE also potentially induces an immune response against the tumor, which may help to guard against metastatic disease development. This study proposes to evaluate the feasibility and safety of treating canine insulinoma with H-FIRE, and to evaluate the tumor immune response to H-FIRE.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE) for treatment of canine insulinoma

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the pain relief effects of novel pain medication, tapentadol, in dogs with bone tumors of the limb. Currently there are limited effective pain medications for treatment of dogs with this disease. What qualifies my pet for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: Have a suspected or confirmed bone tumor (osteosarcoma) of a limb. Be on another oral pain medication (NSAID such as Rimadyl, Previcox or Deramaxx) for at least 3 days prior to starting the study. Dogs with a fracture of their bone tumor or dogs not on another oral pain medication (NSAID) cannot be enrolled in the study. What does enrolling my pet in this clinical trial involve? Your dog will undergo the following procedures: Prior to treatment with the study drug, you will be asked to fill out a baseline pain survey. A veterinarian will also perform a pain assessment and your dog will walk on a pressure sensitive walkway to more objectively assess his or her lameness. Your dog will be sent home with 5 days of the pain medication, after which time your dog will return to the hospital for a repeat of the surveys and procedures described above. Client Compensation Following completion of the study on Day 5, you will receive a $500 credit to be used towards further procedures (diagnostics and/or treatments for your dog's cancer) at OSU VMC.
current_roster.name: Novel anti-cancer drug for dogs with bone tumors (osteosarcoma) that has spread to their lungs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate responses to a standardized protocol using Immunocidin as a palliative therapy and to assess quality of life (QOL) outcomes in dogs diagnosed with solid tumors that are surgically removed before start of the therapy. The information from this trial will be used to develop a palliative care option for dogs whose owners can not afford chemotherapy or elect not to pursue other treatment modalities after the tumors are surgically removed. The main goal of this palliative therapy is to minimize the pets discomfort and improve his/her overall quality of life.
current_roster.name: Use of Immunocidin for palliative therapy in dogs diagnosed with solid tumors

current_roster.description:
Purpose: 
To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and immune effects of using a novel non-thermal ablation technique, high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE), for treating canine lung tumors. Background Canine lung tumors can occur as primary or metastatic tumors. New treatment options are needed for these types of tumors, as patient outcomes are often poor, and survival times have improved little over several decades.

High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that precisely ablates tumors while sparing critical structures. H-FIRE also potentially induces an anti-tumor immune response, which may help to guard against metastatic disease development.This study proposes to evaluate the feasibility and safety of treating canine lung tumors with H-FIRE, and to evaluate the tumor immune response to H-FIRE. Because canine lung tumors are a comparative model for human lung cancer, this work may inform future studies to evaluate the use of H-FIRE in people, ultimately improving outcomes for both humans and dogs.

This study is funded by the Veterinary Memorial Fund. 

Study Design: Dogs with suspected lung tumors will have an initial visit to determine eligibility, including relevant bloodwork, examination, and diagnostic imaging. Once the dog is enrolled, minimally invasive H-FIRE treatment will be administered under CT guidance at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg, VA. Dogs will be transferred to the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center (ACCRC) in Roanoke, VA, where they will be monitored for 72 hours following administration of H-FIRE. Tumor resection surgery will take place at the end of the 72-hour monitoring period, and dogs will remain at the ACCRC until they are fully recovered from surgery, typically 2-3 days. Total hospitalization time for the study is approximately 5-7 days. Compensation For enrolled dogs, the study-related bloodwork, histopathological analysis of the resected tumor, and up to $1,000 of the cost of a CT scan will be paid for by the study. The cost of H-FIRE treatment and post-treatment monitoring is covered by the study. An additional credit of up to $2,000 toward the cost of resection surgery is also provided. For enrolled dogs, owners out of pocket costs, including initial screening to determine eligibility, are estimated at $2,000-4,000.
current_roster.tagline: Canine lung tumor study
current_roster.name: Evaluation of high-frequency irreversible electroporation (H-FIRE) for treatment of canine lung tumors

current_roster.description: Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy drug that has demonstrated a broad spectrum of activity against human and canine cancers. Previously Paclitaxel has not been an option for canine patients due how it was formulated, however a new formulation of Paclitaxel (called Oraxol or Oral Paclitaxel) has now been developed and resolves these issues. Preclinical studies have demonstrated safety in dogs, making Oraxol an intriguing choice for further study in dogs with cancer. This study will be evaluating the tolerability of Oraxol in dogs with cancer when administered as a sole agent. Oraxol will be administered orally at home. If favorable tolerability is demonstrated, this data will be used to include Oraxol in Ethos Discoverys ongoing trial for canine splenic hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma).
current_roster.name: Tolerability of Oral Paclitaxel in Dogs with Cancer

current_roster.description:
Oral malignant melanoma (OMM) is a highly aggressive oral tumor in dogs. The presence of spread to regional lymph nodes (LN) is a known poor prognostic indicator. Evaluation of LN status is currently performed by histopathologic examination following removal of all surgically identifiable LN in the neck region. This study aims to identify the sentinel lymph node (SLN), allowing a targeted approach to reduce the need for extensive LN resection surgery. This study will evaluate removed LNs with a new emerging diagnostic tool, optical coherence tomography (OCT), to determine if OCT imaging findings can accurately detect cancer in canine LNs. In the future, OCT may be used for intraoperative assessment of LN status to guide the extent of LN removal for individual patients.

Patients will undergo routine preoperative staging consistent with current standard of care (bloodwork, thoracic radiographs). All patients enrolled in the study will undergo sedation or general anesthesia for computed tomography (CT) of the head and regional contrast administration for sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping for surgical planning. Following CT, the SLN identified will be sampled using ultrasound guidance. All patients will undergo surgical removal of the primary tumor as well as all surgically identifiable cervical lymph nodes as is current standard of care. Patients are required to be evaluated at 10-14 days post operatively for incision evaluation and 3- and 6-months post operatively for routine restaging chest x-rays.
current_roster.tagline: Lymph node and imaging evaluation in oral melanomas
current_roster.name: Lymph node and imaging evaluation in oral melanomas

current_roster.description: Purpose: Neratinib is an FDA approved drug for treatment of human breast and lung cancer. It can be orally administered and works by blocking the action of a protein called HER2. We have recently determined that approximately 50% of canine lung cancers (pulmonary adenocarcinomas, ADC) carry gene mutations in HER2 identical to those found in human pulmonary adenocarcinoma. The purpose of this study is to perform a clinical trial of neratinib in dogs with ADC carrying HER2 mutations to evaluate effectiveness of this drug. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: Confirmed diagnosis of primary lung carcinoma. Patient must test positive for ERBB2V659E mutation based on tumor aspirate and/or circulating DNA Dogs must be at least 1 year of age and 10 kg. Adequate organ function as indicated by standard laboratory tests Otherwise medically healthy with no clinically significant physical findings upon examination, medical history, and clinical laboratory profile, as deemed by the principal investigators. Prior chemotherapy or radiation must be completed 2 weeks prior to study entry and the patient must have recovered from the acute toxicities of these treatments. What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Enrollment screening requires baseline blood work, urine analysis, chest x-rays, chest ultrasound, a fine needle aspirate of the lung tumor and tumor measurements. Once the HER2 mutation is confirmed in the lung tumor (approximately 5-10 days), your dog will return to receive a computed tomography (CT) of the chest performed under general anesthesia. The following day, your pet will begin therapy with neratinib. It is important to make certain that the drug levels are achieving high enough concentrations to kill the tumor cells. To determine this, your pet will have approximately teaspoon of blood (2 mL or cc) taken through a sterile catheter placed in the front leg at 8 time points dispersed during the first 48 hours while your pet is receiving neratinib. You will return on Day 14 of neratinib treatment and your pet will have another drug level study performed by measuring drug concentrations at 8 time points during a 48 hour period. Additional assessments of organ function (standard clinical chemistries, CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis) will be performed and DNA concentrations while your pet is receiving neratinib will occur every 14 days on Days 28, 42 and 56 of treatment. On Days 28 and the last day of treatment (Day 56) your dog will need to stay for at least 4 hours for chest imaging (CT) performed under general anesthesia. After cessation of neratinib, if your pet still has a pulmonary mass and surgery is an option for removal, you may elect to have this surgery performed at OSU-VMC by a board-certified oncologic surgeon. The study requires that you return to the OSU-VMC with your dog at Days 120, 240, 320 and 480 for continued post-surgical patient and longitudinal tumor burden monitoring through routine blood work and a small sample of blood collected for ctDNA. On Day 480, your dog will receive general anesthesia for thoracic CT to look for progressive disease, if tumor is identified a thoracic ultrasound will be performed and a fine needle aspirate will be performed to collect a small sample of the tumor to look for additional gene mutations. Client Compensation All costs associated with screening and every study visit are covered by the trial. These include patient visits, hemograms, biochemistry profiles, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, thoracic CTs, ultrasound guided fine needle aspirate of the thoracic mass and the cytology interpretation, HER2 mutation test, anesthesia, IV catheter, sample collection and processing costs, hospitalization, loperamide and maripitant drug costs. Additionally, the amount of $3368 for surgery to remove the tumor if applicable is covered by this study. Any medical issues that arise that are not due to the neratinib will not be covered.
current_roster.name: Neratinib in dogs with lung cancer

current_roster.description: This purpose of this pilot study is to evaluate the safety and activity of a STING agonist compound to stimulate the immune system to attack cancer cells in dogs with malignant melanoma, mammary carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma on the head or neck, and high grade soft tissue sarcoma. Other solid tumors may qualify as well. In order to be eligible dogs must: Weigh 33 lbs or more Have a diagnosis of a solid, malignant tumor type such as: Malignant melanoma Mammary carcinoma Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the head or neck High grade soft tissue sarcoma Osteosarcoma (if amenable to repeat biopsy) Prior treatment is permitted as long as there is a measurable tumor present. Anticipated study duration is 6 weeks. The trial includes an initial staging appointment, two immunotherapy treatments requiring overnight stays in the hospital, and surgery. All appointments require the ability to travel to Ryan Veterinary Hospital in Philadelphia, PA and adherence to the study schedule. All study specific visits, including staging and surgery, covered by the study.If interested, call the VCIC department at 215-573-6610 or email the study coordinator, June Chiango, at jchiango@upenn.edu.
current_roster.name: Immunotherapy Clinical Trial for Dogs with Solid Tumors with a Moderate to High Risk of Metastasis

current_roster.description: External beam radiation is often used to relieve pain and control cancer, specifically primary bone cancer (osteosarcoma). It is very effective, but it can cause long-term side effects including swelling, stiffness, pain, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of secondary malignancy. Fracture risk specifically is significant yet poorly understood. We know that a subset of patients, but not all patients, are at a clinically significant increased risk of fracture following radiation therapy. We also know that if a fracture occurs, it can be very difficult to treat. In human medicine such a fracture often requires several operations and many months of recovery. In veterinary medicine, fracture following radiation therapy cannot usually be fixed, requiring an amputation or humane euthanasia. Currently the risk of fracture is assessed based on x-ray characteristics and patient symptoms. However, limited knowledge of the mechanisms or extent of changes in bone secondary to radiation treatment has decreased our ability to mitigate, prevent, or predict complications in both humans and dogs. Our goal is to explore the effects of external beam radiation in a canine model. Dogs are a large animal model for humans, in which the anatomical design, mechanics of movement, and demands of load closely reflect humans. Any discoveries will be relevant and translatable to both humans and dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Palliative Radiation for Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Radiation Therapy on the Strength of Bone

current_roster.description: High-grade glioma is the one of the most common brain tumors in dogs. Many owners are given a hopeless prognosis and offered no treatment when this type of tumor is diagnosed with advanced imaging, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The median survival time of dogs given no definitive therapy is estimated to be 1-2 months. Glioma cells are known to be highly motile cells. We plan on using that characteristic; implanting a catheter lined with nanofibers into the tumor mass to attract and guide tumor cells away from the brain and into an external reservoir. These nanofiber catheters were shown to decrease tumor volume in a laboratory tumor model. All dogs enrolled in the study will be offered more definitive current standard of care therapy for the tumor after the catheter is explanted with the costs (up to $5,000) covered by the study sponsor. An MRI is required prior to enrollment as well as a screening visit at the University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center (VMC). Surgery to place the tumor monorail will take place with dogs remaining in the ICU and hospital wards up to 3 days. Recheck visits are at Day 14, Day 30, Day 60 and Day 90, with MRI and neurological exam, blood and urine sampling, CSF tap (twice possible only). The device will be taken out (explanted) at most at Day 90, and sooner if neurological signs and MRI indicate disease progression. After explantation, standard of care options for the dog will be discussed (surgical debulking or radiation therapy).
current_roster.name: Evaluating the safety of the tumor monorail in a companion canine model

current_roster.description: Overview: In this approach, immune cells (known as T cells) are taken from the peripheral blood, genetically modified in the laboratory to express a receptor that recognizes B cells, and then expanded to produce large numbers of tumor specific T cells outside of the body. These genetically modified (re-directed) T cells are then infused back into the body where they will seek out B cells and kill them. This process is known as adoptive immunotherapy and the cells that are infused into the patients are known as chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR T cells). The approach has shown promising results in people with blood cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). More information about this approach in people can be found here: http://www.nature.com/nri/journal/v12/n4/full/nri3191.html Study Purpose: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of B cell specific CAR T cells to target and kill B cell malignancies. This study uses your dogs own immune cells (T cells) obtained from a peripheral blood sample. Your dogs T cells will be genetically modified in the laboratory to become CART-20 cells designed to recognize, target, and kill CD20+ B cells. Your dog will receive chemotherapy prior to infusion and then CART-20 cells will be infused back into your dog by an intravenous infusion (into a vein). It is hoped that these cells will seek out B cells and kill them, leading to a reduction in tumor burden and clinical remission. Eligibility criteria: Dogs with B cell lymphoma or B cell malignancies. Dogs with confirmed expression of the target molecule (CD20) on the surface of their tumor cells (this can be determined at UPenn). Dogs that weigh more than 10kg. Dogs whose T cells can be successfully grown and genetically modified in the laboratory. Dogs that have no other concurrent medical problems. Comments: At this time, we are enrolling patients in a sequential manner, meaning that the next patient will only be treated after the first patient has finished their course of therapy.
current_roster.name: Re-directed Autologous T cell Therapy for B cell lymphoma or B Cell Leukemia

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to prevent macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib therapy. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of high-dose losartan and toceranib can significantly slow tumor growth and, in some cases, stimulate significant tumor shrinkage in dogs with macroscopic OS lung metastases. More recent studies indicate that the addition of a third, experimental, and immunologically active drug called ladarixin further enhances the activity of the losartan/toceranib combination by blocking recruitment of cancer inducing cells to established microscopic metastases in the lungs. Prior clinical trials deem this 3-drug combination as well-tolerated and safe to use in dogs. The purpose of this trial is to investigate the effectiveness of losartan/toceranib/ladarixin in delaying/preventing the development of macroscopic OS lung metastases. These results will be compared to those from a recently completed trial evaluating the standard chemotherapy drug used after surgery for OS (carboplatin). If this novel combination is shown to be equivalent or superior to carboplatin therapy for delaying/preventing metastatic OS, the findings would exert a major impact on both the veterinary and pediatric osteosarcoma fields, as this 3-drug combination could be readily evaluated in future trials. Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest and affected limb. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. Following enrollment into the trial, your dog will be sent home with oral losartan and ladarixin to be given twice daily and oral toceranib to be given every other day. A biopsy of the bone tumor will also be performed prior to starting treatment providing your dog is deemed to be a good candidate for this procedure. Your dog will then return 10-14 days later for limb amputation. The tumor will be submitted for biopsy evaluation, and the diagnosis of osteosarcoma must be confirmed by this test. Toceranib will be discontinued for 3 days prior to amputation and 7 days post-amputation and will resume on Week 3. Your dog will then return two weeks later (Week 4) for an exam, blood work, and study blood collection. After the Week 4 visit, follow-up visits will be required every month until the Week 52 visit (1 year). Blood will be collected for study purposes (~1.5 tablespoons) at every visit for the study. Chest x-rays will be performed prior to enrollment, 8 weeks after enrollment, and monthly thereafter until Week 24 (6 months); after 6 months, chest x-rays will be performed every 8 weeks. Urine tests and blood pressure will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study. If your dog is deemed to be free of disease after 1 year, drug treatment will be discontinued; however, there will be required follow-up visits for physical exam, bloodwork, and chest x-rays every 2 months for up to 3 years from enrollment. If your dog dies while on the study, a post-mortem examination and tumor collection will be necessary to explain the cause of death. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments.
current_roster.name: Modulating the Tumor Microenvironment in Osteosarcoma: Adjuvant Immunotherapy Combination with Losartan/Toceranib/Ladarixin

current_roster.description: When a person or dog is diagnosed with cancer it is important to determine if the disease has spread throughout the body and to monitor them carefully to see if the therapy they are getting is working. Probably one of the most sensitive ways to look for cancer spread is an imaging method called a PET/CT. In people who have cancer they will often do a PET/CT before treatment, then at a specified time after treatment to try to see if the therapy is working. In veterinary medicine we have been using pre-treatment PET/CTs for about a decade, but we have never really looked to see what a follow up PET/CT can tell us. We want to use this clinical trial to see if we can do these studies to find out if there are cancer cells left in a tumor treated with high doses of radiation. If we can do that our next step in a future clinical trial would be to try and figure out how to also get rid of those cells. On the first day of the study you pet will be placed under anesthesia for imaging. Initially we will do an F18-FDG PET/CT to stage your pet, meaning to find out where the cancer is in the body. This is a special form of imaging that involves giving your pet a small dose of a radioactive substance. The radiation dose is small enough that we expect no harm to be associated with it, and it is a substance that weve given to many dogs without problems. They will be under anesthesia for a few hours for the imaging then recovered in a special area of the hospital until the radioactive substance is almost completely gone. This way your pet will be safe for you to pet and touch. In almost every case that we have done this on (>350 dogs and counting) the dog will be able to go home the same night they had the imaging. While your pet is under anesthesia we may do some samples taken with a small needle from a few lymph nodes or other areas where it looks like cancer may have spread. These areas may include certain organs such as the liver or spleen. If we need to sample these organs we will use an ultrasound to guide us to limit risks as much as possible. After the initial imaging your pet will be treated with radiation and any chemotherapy protocol you and your oncologist have agreed on. Your pet will need to have the same imaging and sampling performed after about 3-4 months after the radiation therapy is complete. In the interim between the PET/CTs one of team members will contact you approximately once a month to ask a short series of questions to see how your pet is doing. After the second PET/CT we will continue to occasionally contact you (probably once every 3-4 months) for updates. We would ask that if any serious medical changes occur with your pet, especially if they have to do with the tumor that has been treated with radiation, that you contact us and update our team.
current_roster.name: F18 FDG PET/CT following radiation therapy

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA) is a highly aggressive bone tumor, with 85-90% of dogs succumbing to their disease due to metastatic spread, most commonly to the lungs. There are no effective treatments for metastatic disease and the current focus of drug development strategies is on prevention of metastases. Interleukin-15 (IL-15) is an immune stimulatory molecule called a cytokine that activates certain cells of the immune system (T-cells and Natural Killer cells). This molecule has been shown to have potent anticancer immune effects in mouse models, and there is preliminary evidence to suggest that immunotherapy with inhaled cytokines can cause large osteosarcoma tumors in the lungs of dogs to shrink. The primary goal of this study is to determine whether inhaled recombinant-human IL-15 (rhIL-15) therapy is effective at delaying the onset of metastasis in dogs with OSA when combined with standard-of-care (definitive surgery and subsequent chemotherapy) while evaluating its safety and tolerability in the post-operative/pre-chemotherapy setting. Data from this trial will be used to assess the feasibility and design of human clinical trials evaluating inhaled delivery of rhIL-15 in patients with lung metastasis. For this study, we ask for your consent to the surgical amputation of your dogs affected limb within 10 days of obtaining eligibility test results. At the time of surgery, tumor and normal tissues samples will be collected and regional lymph nodes removed and assessed for metastasis. Between 1-4 days post-amputation, your dog will begin treatment with twice daily, inhaled rhIL-15. The two treatments should be given 8-12 hours apart. Training of your dog will occur prior to surgery when possible to acclimate him/her to the treatments equipment and procedure. Between 15-21 days post-amputation (minimum 12-hours after completion of the last IL-15 treatment), your dog will begin carboplatin chemotherapy. Carboplatin will be administered every 21 days, for 4 total treatments, at CSU as outpatient procedures. A visit will be required 3 weeks after the last chemotherapy treatment for an exam and chest x-rays, and from then on, your dog will be assessed for lung metastasis every 2 months via chest x-rays. Additional blood samples will be collected at several visits throughout the trial for study purposes. If your dog should die while enrolled in the trial, a necropsy will be required to explain the cause of death.
current_roster.name: COTC030: Evaluation of Inhaled recombinant-human IL-15 combined with Standard-of-Care in dogs with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Local treatment (typically amputation) in conjunction with adjuvant chemotherapy improves disease-free interval (DFI) and overall survival time (OST) in dogs with OS, but approximately 85% of dogs will eventually develop metastatic disease. Current treatment options for metastatic OS are limited to cytotoxic chemotherapy with an average survival time of 60 days. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as inflammatory monocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib therapy. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of high-dose losartan and toceranib can significantly slow tumor growth and, in some cases, stimulate significant tumor shrinkage in dogs with macroscopic OS lung metastases. More recent studies indicate that the addition of a third, experimental and immunologically active drug called ladarixin further enhances the activity of the losartan/toceranib combination by blocking recruitment of cancer inducing cells to established microscopic metastases in the lungs. Prior clinical trials deem this 3-drug combination as well-tolerated and safe to use in dogs. The purpose of this trial is to investigate the safety and biologic activity of losartan/toceranib/ladarixin in dogs with metastatic OS to the lungs, assess the overall response rate and duration of response to this treatment, and determine the effects of treatment on tumor genetics and the immune system. Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. Following enrollment into the trial, your dog will be sent home with oral losartan and ladarixin to be given twice daily and oral toceranib to be given every other day. Recheck visits are required 2 and 4 weeks after starting the drugs and then every 4 weeks. Additional blood will be collected at every visit for study purposes. A complete blood cell count will be performed every visit, and a chemistry panel done every month. Chest x-rays will be performed prior to enrollment and every month thereafter until withdrawal. Urine tests and blood pressure will be performed prior to enrollment and every 8 weeks for the duration of the study. If your dog is deemed to be free of disease after 6 months, drug treatment will still be available but not covered financially by the study. If your dog dies while on the study, a post-mortem examination will be necessary to explain the cause of death. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments.
current_roster.name: Modulating the Tumor Microenvironment in Metastatic Osteosarcoma: Palladia/Losartan/Ladarixin Combination Therapy

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in cats. Current treatment options include various types of chemotherapy; however, there are no approved drugs for lymphoma in cats, very few cats are cured and most will relapse. New drugs remain necessary to treat these drug-resistant relapses. Rabacfosadine is an intravenous chemotherapy agent that has been used both in normal dogs and in more than 80 dogs with cancer. It has been shown to induce remission in 60 to 100% of dogs with lymphoma. It has been administered to 4 healthy cats as a single dose with no adverse effects. The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of rabacfosadine, given once every 21 days, to cats with lymphoid neoplasia. Initially your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests, which may include blood tests, urinalysis, chest X-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and fine needle aspirate of any masses. The results of these initial tests will determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are part of the routine testing done in patients with lymphoid neoplasia, and may be performed even if you decide that your pet will not participate. Your cat will then receive an injection of rabacfosadine every 3 weeks for up to 5treatments. Rechecks will be required 1 week after the first treatment, and possibly 1 week following the second treatment, depending on whether side effects are noted or not. This study does not have a placebo group all cats will receive treatment with rabacfosadine.
current_roster.tagline: Tanovea in Cats with Lymphoid Neoplasia
current_roster.name: VC-009:  Study to Determine the Safety and Efficacy of TANOVEA™ (Rabacfosadine for Injection) in Cats with Lymphoid Neoplasia Usin

current_roster.description: Transitional Cells Carcinoma (TCC, Bladder cancer) comprises approximately 2% of all naturally occurring cancers in dogs, similar to rates in humans. With more than 70 million pet dogs in the United States and cancer developing in approximately 25% of older dogs, it is expected that bladder cancer will newly affect more than 20,000 dogs each year. Our collaborators at University of Iowa developed a novel delivery system for chemotherapeutics for TCC, based on nanoparticles. This technology allows for the treatment(s) to be delivered locally into the bladder, and specifically target the tumor. In this project, we want to test the safety and efficacy of this technique, by comparing the outcome of 2 groups of dogs affected by TCC: One group treated by intravesicular (into the urinary bladder) administration of nanoparticles infused with an anti-cancer drug (vinblastine). One group treated by intravesicular (into the urinary bladder) administration of the same anti-cancer drug (vinblastine) alone. All groups will also be treated orally by Piroxicam (NSAID) during the entire trial, as standard of care.
current_roster.name: New technology tested for dogs with Bladder Cancer

current_roster.description: ENROLLMENT SUSPENDED Purpose To evaluate if treatment with NPS alters immune markers and impacts treatment outcome when combined with standard chemotherapy. Background Large cell lymphoma affecting the peripheral lymph nodes (multicentric) is one of the most common cancers diagnosed in dogs, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype. DLBCL in dogs is clinically and genetically similar to DLBCL in people; clinical trials in dogs are helping to identify new treatments to benefit both dogs and people diagnosed with this cancer. One of cancers strategies is to evade the immune system by suppressing immune cell recognition and the ability of these immune cells to kill cancer cells. Treatments that address this by using drugs, antibodies, or directly training a patients immune system, are becoming common in people, but we are far from curing lymphoma in dogs or people. The use of local ablative strategies to modify the immune system (AIM, or ablative immune modification) and shift it from a suppressed to an active environment has been shown to be effective in rodent models and people with other cancer types. The purposes of this study are 1.) to evaluate the impact on the number and types of immune cells and their gene expression following a single treatment to a lymph node in dogs with DLBCL, and 2.) whether NPS pre-treatment prolongs the remission time when treated with standard chemotherapy with doxorubicin. Study Design This study takes place at the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center (ACCRC) in Roanoke, VA.This is a prospective, single-blind, randomized, proof-of-principle clinical trial. Dogs will be randomized to either AIM (treatment with NPS), or placebo. Only the investigation team will know whether your dog has received AIM (NPS). Blood and lymph node needle biopsies will be obtained periodically throughout the study to monitor the immune response. All dogs will undergo standard chemotherapy treatment with doxorubicin following AIM (NPS) or placebo. Chemotherapy will be given under the direct supervision of a board-certified veterinary medical oncologist at the ACCRC. If you agree to participate in the study, we will perform the following procedures: (a) Pretreatment evaluation (screening, prior to enrollment)Before beginning treatment, your dog must undergo the following tests to determine if s/he is a good candidate to enroll in the study. 1. Complete physical exam 2. Lab work 3. Biopsy or fine needle aspirate of a lymph node read by a pathologist 4. Special testing to identify whether the lymphoma is B-cell or T-cell (immunophenotyping by flow cytometry) 5. Thoracic and abdominal imaging (b) Treatment Once your dog is enrolled in the study, there are (13) protocol clinic visits which include (1) NPS or placebo treatment under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, (5) chemotherapy treatments, (2) imaging visits, (13) blood draws, and (8) fine needle aspirates (needle biopsy) of a lymph node. Upon completion of the chemotherapy protocol, monthly exams are required to monitor for remaining in complete remission: the number of these visits will vary. Nanopulse stimulation is short bursts of electrical fields applied directly to the lymph node. It is considered painless in humans and does not generate heat. NPS treatment is expected to take 30-45 minutes. Compensation The study covers the sedation and NPS (or placebo) treatment, the collection and analysis of blood and lymph node samples for determining immune response, and $250 per chemotherapy treatment visit.The total compensation per patient enrolled is $1,430.All other costs associated with screening, the chemotherapy treatment and monitoring visits, required imaging exams at day 49, and any medications or hospital visits necessary for managing side effects are out-of-pocket. All diagnostics or procedures not covered by the study are standard, and would be performed in any pet dog undergoing evaluation and treatment for lymphoma with chemotherapy. The out-of-pocket costs may vary during the study period. As of July 1, 2021, the screening costs are estimated to be $1000-1200, the costs of imaging are estimated to be $500-700. The cost of treatments vary based on your dogs weight, and management of side effects also greatly varies. Estimates of treatment visits will be calculated specifically for your dog and provided at the time of screening.
current_roster.name: Nanopulse Stimulation for dogs with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: Sinonasal caner is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed rogress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to investigate the local immune response following stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) and determine whether concurrent administration of two immune-modulating drugs, losartan and propranolol, improves positive anti-tumor immune responses in dogs with sinonasal carcinoma. Dogs enrolled into this study will be randomized to one of two groups: the first group will receive SBRT in combination with oral losartan and propranolol, and the other group will be treated with SBRT alone. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush and tumor biopsy under anesthesia. If your dog is randomized to the treatment group, he/she will receive treatment with losartan and propranolol for a minimum of 7 days prior to starting radiation therapy. All dogs will receive 3 treatments with SBRT given on consecutive days. Dogs will then return two weeks after SBRT for a physical exam and anesthesia for a nasal flush and tumor biopsy. Three, 6, 12, & 18 months after completion of SBRT, dogs will return for blood work, urinalysis, and CT scan to evaluate tumor response to treatment. A small amount of blood will also be collected for study purposes prior to treatment and at the 2-week, 3-month, and 6-month post-treatment visits. Tear production will also be tested prior to treatment and at all post-treatment visits.
current_roster.tagline: Radiation +/- Immunotherapy for Dogs with Nasal Carcinoma
current_roster.name: Local immune response to radiation therapy and combined myeloid cell targeted therapy in a dog model of sinonasal carcinoma

current_roster.description: This study will test intra-tumor delivery of vectors that produce an immune signaling molecule, IL-12, (via injection of ZVex12 or IL12srRNA) to deliver sustained IL-12 production in the tumor to stimulate anti-tumor immunity to treat dogs with sarcoma. ZVex12 and IL12srRNA will both result in an inflammatory sarcoma tumor microenvironment. Through this trial, it is expected that we will determine if increased T cells (anti-tumor immune cells) are present in sarcoma tumors following intra-tumor treatment. Two groups of participants will be assigned by randomization 3 dogs being injected with ZVex12 (along with ultrasound, if needed) and 3 dogs being injected with IL12srRNA (along with ultrasound, if needed). Regardless of assigned group, all dogs in the study will be evaluated (to determine eligibility) through blood tests, urinalysis, CT scan with tumor biopsy, and surgery to remove the tumor.
current_roster.name: IL-12

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: The purposes of this study are to find out:How often lymph nodes in the neck contain cancer in dogs undergoing surgery to remove a thyroid tumor.If special stains improve detection of cancer within lymph nodes compared to standard staining.The impact of cancer within lymph nodes on survival in affected dogs.The accuracy of CT for detection of lymph node involvement.
current_roster.name: Thyroid Lymph node Met Study

current_roster.description: Purpose To determine the efficacy and side effect profile of THOP, a new multi-drug chemotherapy protocol, as the first-line treatment in dogs with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Background Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers diagnosed in dogs. The current standard of care for treatment is a chemotherapy protocol that uses multiple drugs: doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone. This protocol, the UW-19, requires weekly clinic visits for 19 weeks, and is the most effective treatment available: >85% of dogs experience a complete clinical remission (all enlarged lymph nodes return to normal size). However, canine lymphoma is rarely cured: less than 10% of dogs are alive at two years after diagnosis. Half of dogs treated with the UW-19 will have a complete remission for longer than 8-10 months. However, the remission time is measured from the date of diagnosis to the date of cancer progression, which includes the 5 months of treatment, resulting in 3-5 months of life in remission after finishing the treatment protocol. Multiple attempts to reduce the treatment time using the same combination of drugs have failed. Our team proposes a different strategy: replacing the least effective drug in the UW-19, cyclophosphamide, with a more effective drug, temozolomide. We will reduce the total treatment time from 19 weeks to 15 weeks by giving temozolomide at the same time as doxorubicin. Temozolomide has been shown to be work well alongside doxorubicin, and to be effective in dogs whose lymphoma does not respond, or stops responding, to standard of care protocols, like the UW-19. The objective of our study is to determine the efficacy and side effect profile of THOP, a new multi-drug chemotherapy protocol, as the first-line treatment in dogs with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). This approach will reduce the treatment time by 4 weeks and the overall cost of treatment by more than $1,000. Compensation Enrollment in the study will provide the temozolomide at no charge (approximately $500-1,000), the cost of the imaging exams at week 6 (approximately $600), and $300 credit to be applied towards out-of-pocket costs. All other costs associated with THOP treatment and monitoring are out-of-pocket, including the screening (eligibility) tests, imaging exams, clinic or hospital visits for medical management of side effects, and follow-up visits. For qualifying owners who agree to participate, the cost of flow cytometry to help determine the type of lymphoma ($167) may be covered bya related research study.All diagnostics or procedures are standard, and would be performed in any pet dog undergoing evaluation and treatment for lymphoma with chemotherapy; there are no additional tests or procedures required due to study involvement. The out-of-pocket costs may vary during the study period, and the cost of treatments vary based on the drug that is given and your dogs weight. Estimates of screening tests, treatment visits, and imaging visits (chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound) will be calculated specifically for your pet and provided at the time of screening. You are responsible for any other clinical fees associated with medical complications of the THOP therapy or other medical problems.
current_roster.name: THOP chemotherapy protocol as front-line treatment of canine B-cell lymphoma

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers encountered in dogs. While chemotherapy is initially effective in many dogs with lymphoma, a very small percentage (<1%) of dogs can develop side effects caused by the rapid destruction of a huge number of tumor cells very quickly after the very first treatment. We think that more dogs may develop small changes related to tumor cell destruction in the first 24 hours after the first treatment, that are detectable by laboratory tests but not severe enough to cause serious illness, and that these changes could be predictive of how effective treatment may be. The primary objective of this study is to measure changes in blood gas parameters (lactate, pH) and changes in plasma inflammatory hormones, for the first 24 hours after starting chemotherapy in dogs with lymphoma, and correlate these changes with changes in lymph node size measured 24 hours and 7 days after the start of treatment. If you have elected to treat your dog with the standard, multi-agent chemotherapy protocol we recommend for dogs with lymphoma (CHOP), your dog will receive a standard dose of vincristine as the first treatment. They will spend the night in our Intermediate Care Unit so that their vital signs (temperature, pulse, respiration) can be measured and blood collected (approximately 2 teaspoons per time point) multiple times overnight (2, 4, 8 and 24 hours after vincristine is given). After 24 hours, your dog will be discharged and will return 1 week following treatment for collection of additional blood and lymph node measurement.
current_roster.name: Incidence of Subclinical Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Dogs with Multicentric Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Purpose To investigate whether genetic material (DNA and microRNA) from cancer cells can be identified in the blood of dogs and cats with lymphoma. Background A few techniques are available to diagnose lymphoma, the most common blood-related cancer in dogs and cats. However, these techniques may fail to provide a definitive diagnosis, or the collection of samples may not be possible because of tumor location, financial constraints, or the patient's clinical condition. Small fragments of genes (also called DNA) and other regulatory molecules (also called microRNA) usually are present in the blood in minimal amounts. Therefore, when an animal has cancer, both the DNA and microRNA of the cancerous cells will also circulate in the blood. This study aims to perform whole-genome and microRNA sequencing in the tissues of dogs and cats diagnosed with lymphoma. Then, we will investigate whether these same DNA mutations and microRNA signatures can also be identified in the patient's blood. In the future, we plan to follow patients along their treatment and post-treatment phases to evaluate if these biomarkers will be associated with disease progression or remission during chemotherapy and whether they will predict the patient's outcome.
current_roster.name: Investigating if genetic material from cancer cells can be found in the blood of dogs and cats with lymphoma

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is the most common bone tumor found in the dog. While we can manage the primary disease with surgery and chemotherapy, the disease in most dogs will eventually spread to other organs, most commonly the lungs. The prognosis for dogs with metastasis is dismal with expected survival measured in days to weeks, so safe and effective therapies are needed to manage this condition. We are evaluating a new combination therapy using a genetically modified Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV-IFN-NIS, or "VSV") plus a new molecule that increases anti-tumor immunity, called onco-immune accelerator or "ONIx" for dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma. Dogs will not receive additional chemotherapy while they are enrolled in the study, but they will be eligible to add chemotherapy or pursue other treatments if their tumors grow and cause signs of illness while on the METEOR protocol.
current_roster.name: METEOR: Dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: This clinical trial evaluates the response toan experimental form of chemotherapy called IF7-SN38. IF7 is a seven-amino acid peptide and SN38 is a metabolite of irinotecan, a cytotoxic drug that has been used as a chemotherapeutic for over two decades. This therapy is scheduled as a series of intravenous treatments given every other day for three to five total treatments.
current_roster.tagline: Brain cancer treatment, metastatic cancer treatment
current_roster.name: Chemotherapy for Canine Cancer Including Metastatic Cancer

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Palliative radiation therapy can provide significant pain relief for dogs who present with lameness and pain caused by osteosarcoma; however, the addition of bisphosphonates to radiation therapy is frequently recommended but without concrete evidence that it provides additional benefit. Anecdotally, improvement in pain response has been reported in children and young adults that receive chemotherapy for osteosarcoma. Similar effects have also been reported in dogs. In the veterinary literature, there are limited studies that support an improvement in onset to response of pain relief, improvement in duration of pain relief, and improvement in survival time when chemotherapy is combined with palliative radiation therapy. With this trial we aim to answer the questions of whether the addition of bisphosphonates or carboplatin chemotherapy provides improved pain relief from bone tumors compared to palliative radiation alone.
current_roster.tagline: Palliative Radiation Therapy With or Without Bisphosphonates or Carboplatin for Bone Cancer in Dogs
current_roster.name: Palliative Radiation Therapy With or Without Bisphosphonates or Carboplatin for Dogs with Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety and ability of copanlisib to prolong survival times in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. We have found that hemangiosarcoma is frequently driven by mutations in a gene called PI3K and that this leads to the cancer cells growing. The drug copanlisib inhibits the PI3K gene pathway and as such it may slow down the growth of cancer cells.In contrast to standard of care chemotherapy, copanlisib should specifically target cells with the PI3K mutation blocking their ability to grow and divide. The overall study design includes a dose escalation scheme to determine the most effective and best tolerated dose of copanlisib. Each patient will be assigned to a specific dose of copanlisib which will be given once a week for three weeks and then one week off. This 4 week cycle will be repeated for a total of four cycles. Once four cycles are completed, the patients will have 5 follow-up visits over the first year to determine whether the cancer has returned. All costs related to the study, including the drug, will be covered by the study.
current_roster.name: Use of the PI3K inhibitor copanlisib to treat splenic hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: Insulinoma is the most common cancer of the pancreas in dogs. Insulinomas have a high rate of metastasis (spread) to other areas of the body including the adjacent lymph nodes, liver, and elsewhere. The treatment of choice is surgical removal of the primary tumor and sites of metastasis, when possible.The aim of this study is to improve detection of surgical margins and metastatic lymph nodes at the time of surgery to remove the tumor. This is vital in both veterinary and human surgical oncology to minimize the chance of local recurrence. We are using a new near-infrared imaging agent injected intravenously and a novel imaging system to identify the tumor and its margins during surgery. This imaging adds no more than 15 minutes to a surgical procedure.
current_roster.name: Cathepsin-activated near-infrared (NIR) imaging for intraoperative detection of insulinomas

current_roster.description: Aims to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative out comes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer.
current_roster.name: Ethos-PUSH

current_roster.description: Goal is to assesses the safety and effectiveness of TdCyd and Aza-TdC, novel anticancer agents, when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent.
current_roster.name: COTC027

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study will be to assess the safety and efficacy of CAR-T cells constructed from human cells to treat large B cell lymphoma in dogs. CAR-T cells are lymphocytes (immune cells) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of any cell carrying the target molecule. This study will seek to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on the tumor, as well as the dogs immune system.
current_roster.name: Leah Labs xCAR-T

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate the safety and feasibility of treating oral tumors in dogs using a novel iontophoretic system to deliver chemotherapy directly to the tumor site. Background Canine oral tumors come in many forms and can vary widely in prognosis, depending on tumor location, tumor type, tumor size, and presence of metastatic spread. The two most common cancerous tumor types are malignant melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma. For these cancers, the best outcomes are achieved if surgeons can remove all the tumor with clean margins. Factors such as tumor location, tumor size and invasion of adjacent structures such as bone affect whether or not surgical removal is feasible. Radiation therapy is recommended after surgery when the tumor is incompletely excised or in some occasions in gross (visible) disease, where surgery is not feasible. Systemic chemotherapy alone hasnt been effective at treating oral tumors in dogs. Carboplatin is the most common drug used and the one that has shown some efficacy when the disease has spread. Chemotherapy is usually part of a multimodal treatment protocol; either starting after surgery to address metastatic disease or given concurrently with radiation therapy as a radio-sensitizer. In this study, were testing a medical device that can deliver chemotherapy drugs directly to the tumor. We hope that by delivering treatment straight to the tumor site, we can increase the effectiveness of chemotherapy. This could be important, especially in cases where surgery isnt a good option. The device used in this study has been used successfully in other cancers, but has never been tried before in dogs with oral cancer. This study is funded byFocal Medical.
current_roster.tagline: Oral tumors in dogs
current_roster.name: Treating oral tumors (malignant melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma) using a new device that delivers chemo directly to the tumor

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917(EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine/piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma.

To determine eligibility for this study, a basic screening visit including a physical exam, blood work, chest X-rays, a fecal exam for parasites, urinalysis, and potentially a genetic test for breeds (shepherds, sheepdogs, collies, old English sheepdogs) at high risk for carrying a mutation that increases the risk of side effects with some chemotherapy drugs will be conducted. All dogs enrolled will receive standard treatment for bladder cancer including vinblastine (a chemotherapeutic delivered intravenously) and piroxicam (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug given daily by mouth). Half the dogs enrolled in this study will be assigned to receive a probiotic (given daily by mouth) in addition to the standard-of-care therapy.

The other half of the dogs will be assigned to receive a placebo (given daily by mouth). Dogs will then undergo a standard treatment regime that includes bloodwork weekly to monitor for low white blood cell counts and IV infusions of vinblastine every 2 weeks unless contraindicated. On the first and last day of the trial, dogs will also undergo sedation/anesthesia for ultrasound and tumor measurement, cystoscopy (visualization of the inside of the bladder), biopsy (tissue collection) from the tumor, and urine collection from the bladder. Owners will be asked to provide free-catch urine and stool samples from their dog every 2 weeks and asked to complete regular questionnaires and logs of the dog's clinical signs and behavior. Owners will also be asked to provide follow-up urine and fecal samples 8 weeks after the trial conclusion.


Client Compensation:

For dogs that meet enrollment criteria and enroll in this study, screening, and subsequent medical management of your dog's bladder cancer for 8 weeks or up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy will be covered at no cost to the owner/agent. The probiotic/placebo will also be provided free of charge for the duration of the study(approximately 8 weeks or for up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy). Limited funding is also available to cover adverse events secondary to the treatment protocol and in accordance with your veterinary team's recommendations. Treatment for following the conditions will be covered as part of this clinical trial during the clinical trial period: Neutropenia, urinary tract infections (UTI) and UTI workups, vomiting/diarrhea. The owner/agent is financially responsible for all veterinary costs unrelated to bladder cancer management (e.g. food, heartworm medication, medications for other conditions). Owners are also financially responsible for all costs associated with bladder cancer management beyond the trial (e.g. after 8 weeks of treatment or 4 rounds of chemotherapy) and for diagnostics and treatments associated with presumed tumor progression. Owners are also financially responsible for adverse events or injuries unrelated to bladder cancer treatment/management.
current_roster.tagline: Probiome Canine Bladder Cancer Clinical Trial
current_roster.name: Probiome for Canine Bladder Cancer

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Probiome Trial for dogs with Bladder Cancer
current_roster.name: Probiome Trial: Can probiotics improve outcomes in canine bladder cancer?

current_roster.description: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is an important protein necessary for the repair of DNA in cells. Cancer cells express a unique type of PCNA (termed caPCNA) which is only found at small quantities in non-cancer cells. Targeting caPCNA with drugs holds promise as a novel therapeutic option with potential for widespread use across multiple cancer types and the possibility of a low risk for side effects. The compound being studied here is a caPCNA inhibitor and has been tested at various doses in healthy dogs with the only side effect noted being diarrhea at higher doses. We now propose a study to investigate the tolerability of this compound in dogs with cancer with the goal of then advancing this drug into future clinical trials that evaluate its use for specific cancer types. The study duration is 35 days and consists of a total of 7 hospital visits. The trial is fully funded with no costs to the owner.
current_roster.name: Tolerability of a novel PCNA inhibitor in tumor-bearing dogs

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study will be to assess the safety of administration of EARLI-201 in dogs with known cancer as well as in normal healthy dogs. The secondary objective of this study is to measure how EARLI-201 distributes in the body and determine if it identify known cancer when used in combination with the 18F-FHBG radionuclide labeled tracer.
current_roster.name: EARLI

current_roster.description: The main role of the thyroid glands is to produce thyroid hormones. Iodine is needed to produce these hormones and the sodium iodide symporter is an essential part of how thyroid cells take up iodine. Thyroid cells can sometimes become cancerous. Many of these thyroid tumors are controlled with surgery alone, but some may either come back within the neck or at distant sites, such as the lungs. A combination of surgery and radioactive iodine is commonly used in people with high risk, differentiated thyroid cancer to decrease the risk of thyroid cancer coming back. This combination has also been associated with good outcomes in dogs with thyroid cancer. Unfortunately, not all thyroid tumors in dogs take up iodine and identifying this currently requires expensive imaging before surgery that is not widely available. The primary purpose of this study will be to assess whether using special stains for the sodium iodide symporter can allow us to identify tumors that are taking up iodine after a thyroid tumor has been removed. This would limit the need for expensive thyroid scans before surgery and increase the number of dogs that could be considered for additional treatment if their thyroid cancer is aggressive
current_roster.name: Sodium Iodine Symporter

current_roster.description: A multicenter, randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled clinical trial to evaluate a novel investigational product in dogs with stage 3 and stage 4 intranasal adenocarcinoma.
current_roster.tagline: Intranasal adenocarcinoma
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial for Canine Intranasal Adenocarcinoma

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is the most common malignancy in cats and small cell gastrointestinal T cell lymphoma represents a large proportion of lymphoma diagnoses in middle age to older cats. The chemotherapy drug chlorambucil is routinely prescribed to manage small cell gastrointestinal lymphoma, however, the pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) or PK of this drug in cats has not been extensively studied. Compounded formulations of chlorambucil are frequently prescribed to veterinary patients in the United States as this allows for more accurate dosing of the medication to our smaller patients. However, we have previously demonstrated that the potency of compounded formulations of oral chemotherapy medications may differ by more than 10% of the labelled strength. This discrepancy in dosing could lead to under- or over-dosing of patients. To understand the potential clinical impact that use of compounded formulations may have in cats with lymphoma, a foundational understanding of the PK properties and relative bioavailability (how much active drug is absorbed by the body) of compounded chlorambucil is essential.In this study, we seek to better understand the PK, relative bioavailability, and potency of compounded formulations of chlorambucil in cats with small cell GI lymphoma. The night before their visit, cats will need to be fasted starting at midnight but can have access to water. The day of their visit, cats will get a physical exam and an intravenous catheter will be placed to facilitate blood collection through the day. They will be given their first dose of oral compounded chlorambucil and then have blood drawn at four set time periods throughout the day. Once the final blood sample is collected, cats will be released back to their owners to go home. Study participation will be complete after this visit.
current_roster.tagline: Pharmacokinetics of Compounded Chlorambucil in Cats with Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of Compounded Chlorambucil in Cats with Lymphoma

current_roster.description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. pPs can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour. 

 

pPs-enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study offers a novel approach to the treatment of OCSCC in cats. The use of pPs is ground-breaking translational research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2024.
current_roster.tagline: Exploring a Nanoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
current_roster.name: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats

current_roster.description:
This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of ch45H1, a novel anticancer agent, when given to dogs with cancer. This medication is designed to help your dog’s immune system fight their cancer. The data from this study will be used to assist in the development of additional novel cancer agents in humans.

ch45H1 will be given by intravenous (IV, injection into the vein) infusion to your dog on Days 1, 22, 43, and 64 (once every 3 weeks) for a total of 4 doses. This drug is given over 90 minutes following pre-treatment with an anti-nausea medication (ondansetron), a histamine blocker (diphenhydramine), and intravenous fluids.

Within this study, we ask that you permit serial biopsies of your dog’s tumor. A biopsy will be collected prior to the first dose of drug (pre-treatment), on Day 29 and possibly on Day 85, depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general. Your dog will return to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital on Days 21 and 22, 29, 42 and 43, 63 and 64, and 85. Serial blood collections will occur on Days 1, 21-22, 42-43, and 63-64 of the study. Single time point collections will occur on Day 29. Chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be performed for staging purposes prior to treatment and at Days 42 and 85.

If your dog’s cancer responds well to the treatment they receive, you will be asked to participate in an additional follow-up period of up to one (1) years’ time. During that time, you will need to continue to regularly (every 8 weeks) visit the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for examination, tumor evaluation (chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and blood collection. At the conclusion of the study, your dog will undergo a final tumor biopsy.
current_roster.tagline: COTC031a: Novel Immune Therapy for Dogs with Lymphoma or Solid Tumors
current_roster.name: COTC031: Novel Immune Therapy for Dogs with Lymphoma or Solid Tumors

current_roster.description:
Cancer cells have a unique metabolism that is highly dependent on the abundance of glucose. Recent studies in mice have shown that calorie restriction slows cancer progression and improves response to chemotherapy. Other studies in dogs and people have also shown that short-term fasting can reduce chemotherapy side effects. It is not clear yet why this happens, but it is suspected that fasting positively impacts a patient's immune system and how it responds to their cancer. The purpose of this study is to learn more about how the tissue environment and immune responses that surround a tumor might be changed by short-term (48-hour) fasting.


Dogs will be screened at the screening visit (day -14 to day -1) and eligible dogs will be randomized and enrolled on Day 0 at which point a continuous glucose monitor and baseline clinical data will be collected; fasting, if applicable, will begin. All dogs will remain in the hospital starting on day 0 through Day 2 during which blood, urine, feces, and rectal and oral swabs will be collected. Day 2 (48 hours post fasting) will mark the completion of study participation and then care will be transferred to the surgical team for surgical excision per standard of care and discharge to owners.
