The duration of the study is 48 hours.

For dogs that meet all the criteria to participate, the cost of the initial biopsy, the hospitalization for the fasting period and all the related lab work and sample collection for the two-day study will be paid for by the study. These dogs and their owners will also receive $500 to use toward their dog's cancer treatment at the OSU Veterinary Medical Center.
current_roster.tagline: Fasting OSA/OM
current_roster.name: Can short-term fasting produce a favorable tissue immune response to help fight cancer?
current_roster.top_investigator: Shay Bracha, DVM, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation of the affected limb followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months after completing the initial series. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.
current_roster.tagline: Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine
current_roster.name: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description:
Mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common malignant cutaneous tumor in dogs. While surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for most MCT, a subset has a high potential for eventual recurrence and metastasis and require systemic medical therapy following surgery in an attempt to delay or prevent eventual metastasis. Furthermore, some dogs may present with disease that is not amenable to resection owing to size, location, or multifocal or disseminated disease. Medical therapy for these patients remains suboptimal. Gilvetmab is a drug that works by targeting key regulators of the immune system and is conditionally approved for use in dogs. Toceranib phosphate (TOC, PalladiaTM) is a targeted therapy that is approved for use in dogs with MCT. Both gilvetmab and TOC have some reported activity against MCT in the gross disease setting; however, the combination has not been evaluated for safety or efficacy in any tumor type.

The primary objective of this study is to characterize the antitumor effects and adverse effect profile of combined treatment with gilvetmab and toceranib in dogs with measurable MCT.

All dogs will be treated with TOC (oral medication given every other day) and gilvetmab (given as an IV infusion every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. They will also have concurrent treatment with certirizine and omeprazole. Visits will be required every 2 weeks until the week 20 visit. CBC only will be performed for the first 2 visits, and CBC, chemistry profile, UA/UPC, BP +/- imaging will be done every 6 weeks. If dogs have a complete response at the week 20 visit (i.e. tumor is no longer present), they will stop all treatment and come for monitoring visits every 6 weeks. Dogs whose tumors are still present will continue on TOC and recheck every 6 weeks for diagnostics. If at any point your dog’s disease progresses or they experience unacceptable side effects from the study medications, they will be withdrawn from the clinical trial.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment Combination for Dogs with Mast Cell Tumor
current_roster.name: Combination Therapy with Gilvetmab and Toceranib in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description: This study is enrolling dogs in a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness of transdermal ondansetron for the prevention of nausea and vomiting in dogs undergoing chemotherapy with doxorubicin.
current_roster.tagline: Dogs Scheduled to Receive Doxorubicin Chemotherapy
current_roster.name: Dogs Scheduled to Receive Doxorubicin Chemotherapy

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of bendamustine at different doses in dogs with lymphoma.

Bendamustine is a chemotherapy drug that is used to treat various types of cancer in people, including lymphoma. This drug has not been evaluated in dogs with cancer. This drug has been evaluated in healthy dogs at doses similar to the lower doses used in this study and was well-tolerated.

Different doses of bendamustine will be given to dogs in this study. The first group of dogs will get the lowest dose. If the study drug does not cause serious side effects, the next group of dogs will get a higher dose. The study doctor will watch each group carefully as they increase the dose. The doses will continue to increase for each group of dogs until there are side effects that require the dose to be lowered. Once this dose is found, the study is stopped.
current_roster.tagline: Bendamustine for Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma
current_roster.name: Bendamustine for Dogs with Relapsed Lymphoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Matthew Atherton, BVSc, PhD, DECVIM (Oncology)

current_roster.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.
current_roster.tagline: Changes in Bone Density Following Radiation Treatment in Dogs with Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description:
Trial Overview

ELIAS Animal Health is currently conducting a study to assess safety and efficacy of ELIAS’s vaccine-enhanced adoptive T cell therapy combined with a novel adjuvant as a limb-sparing treatment for large-breed dogs newly diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma. The study, which will be funded by a grant from Morris Animal Foundation, will be conducted in collaboration with Dr. Jeffrey Bryan and Dr. Megan Mickelson at the University of Missouri-Columbia.


Trial Summary

  1. Treatment includes limb-sparing surgery to remove primary tumor, followed by vaccine-enhanced adoptive T cell therapy combined with a novel adjuvant.
  2. Patients must complete the 7-11 week protocol, conducted at the University of Missouri Veterinary School of Medicine, and return for periodic follow-up visits.
  3. Each patient will be monitored for 12 months post-diagnosis.
current_roster.tagline: Osteosarcoma Trial for Large Breed Dogs
current_roster.name: ELIAS Osteosarcoma Trial for Large Breed Dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Jeffrey Bryan, Board-Certified Specialist in Veterinary Oncology

current_roster.description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.


There will be two study groups:


The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.


The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
current_roster.tagline: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
current_roster.name: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs

current_roster.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.
current_roster.tagline: Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography for surgical margin assessment for mammary tumors
current_roster.name: Mammary tumors in cats
current_roster.top_investigator: Laura Selmic, MPH, DACVS-SA, DECVS, Surgical Oncology

current_roster.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.
current_roster.tagline: Electrochemotherapy for Bone cancers
current_roster.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

current_roster.description:
B cell lymphoma impacts >250,000 dogs every year. The current standard of care is CHOP chemotherapy, a multi-agent protocol that takes 3-4 months of trips to the vet and costs $7,000-12,000 while only extending the life of a pet 10-12 months.


This clinical trial is evaluating the safety and efficacy of Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in dogs with B cell lymphoma. CAR-T cells are a type of engineered T cell (an immune cell found in mammals) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of cancer cells expressing certain shapes, called antigens. In this trial for B cell lymphoma, the antigen the CAR-T cells will target is called CD20. CAR-T cell therapy is FDA approved for multiple blood cancers in humans and is a revolution in how cancer is treated, bringing cures to patients who have no other treatment options.


This clinical trial seeks to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on lymph node tumors and internal disease, as well as how CAR-T cells influence the dog’s immune system to re-activate and fight cancer on its own. The trial will also test different pre-treatments, determined based on the additive measurements of four target lymph nodes (called the "sum of longest diameters").


This trial is sponsored by LEAH Labs, a biotechnology company building living therapies for pets with cancer. The trial is 100% funded from enrollment, provides a generous adverse event stipend, and offers a stipend for future care.
current_roster.tagline: CAR-T cell therapy for canine B cell lymphoma
current_roster.name: Direct lymph node injection of CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with CD20+ diffuse large B cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: This is an open-label, pilot study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of Cowpea Mosaic Virus (CPMV) administered as an intratumoral injection in dogs with mast cell tumor, soft tissue sarcoma, melanoma, and thyroid tumors. CPMV will be administered as an injection into the tumor once weekly for 4 weeks. If there is >/= 25% reduction in tumor size, an additional 4 doses may be administered for a total of 8 doses. Dogs may have their tumors removed at the end of the initial 4 treatments or after 8 treatments. Hepatic and renal function tests will be monitored on the first day, at day 7 and 2,4, 6, and 8 weeks post starting treatment. Dogs will also undergo weekly physical examinations for any physical changes while on study. The tumor will undergo a biopsy before treatment, at day 14, and surgical resection will be considered at the end of study.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluation of Weekly Intratumoral Cowpea Mosaic Virus in Dogs with Solid Tumors.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Intratumoral Cowpea Mosaic Virus in Dogs with Solid Tumors
current_roster.top_investigator: Ashish Ranjan, BVsc, PhD, Vice Chair Research Innovations Comp. Oncology

current_roster.description: This is an open-label, pilot study evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of radiation therapy combined with histotripsy in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. Radiation therapy will be delivered at once a week for 3 weeks and will be combined with histotripsy delivered twice a week performed 24-72 hours after radiation therapy, applied to the primary tumor using a clinical-grade histotripsy system and image guided targeting (ultrasound). Dogs may have their tumors removed at the end the study. Hepatic and renal function tests will be monitored on the first day and every other week along with physical examinations and owner interviews. The tumor will undergo a biopsy before treatment, and every other week to evaluate changes in the tumor microenvironment. This study is approved by the UT Southwestern Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluation of Combined Radiation Therapy and Histotripsy in Dogs with Sarcomas
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Combined Radiation and High Frequency Ultrasound in dogs with Soft Tissue Sarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Ashish Ranjan, BVsc, PhD, Vice Chair Research Innovations Comp. Oncology

current_roster.description: Dogs with bone cancer or osteosarcoma of the limbs will be first assessed with a specialized imaging called 18F-FDG PET-CT to determine that the tumor is limited to the leg. Once enrolled, the dog will be treated with an immunotherapy directly in the tumor followed by chemotherapy the next 1-2 days prior to amputation. The goal of this therapy is to increase the immune response to the tumor. After amputation, treatment with standard chemotherapy will be augmented with an immune checkpoint inhibitor. At three, six, and twelve months after amputation, non-invasive imaging will be performed to look for spread of osteosarcoma. All treatments performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD are free-of-charge. The immune checkpoint inhibitor will be provided free-of-charge. The owner will need to make arrangements for amputation and chemotherapy with a surgeon and medical oncologist, respectively.

current_roster.name: Immune treatment of Canine Bone Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dara L Kraitchman, VMD, PhD, Professor of Radiology and Director CIGAT

current_roster.description:
In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. 


This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:

  1. Bloodwork for general health screening
  2. Chest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatment
  3. Bone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target protein
  4. Cellular therapy with iNKT cells
  5. Amputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalization
  6. Standard of care chemotherapy
  7. Follow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographs


All clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
current_roster.tagline: CLINCIAL TRIAL FOR DOGS WITH NEWLY DIAGNOSED OSTEOSARCOMA
current_roster.name: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Nicola Mason BVetMed, PhD, DACVIM, FRCVS, Professor of Veterinary Medicine

current_roster.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.
current_roster.tagline: Intra-tumoral T-cell Engager Therapy for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma
current_roster.name: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
current_roster.top_investigator: Kristen Couto, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), Veterinary Oncologist

current_roster.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Radiation for Transmissible Venereal Tumor in Dogs
current_roster.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
current_roster.top_investigator: Kathryn Wolfert, DVM, Medical Oncology resident

current_roster.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.
current_roster.tagline: New Treatment for Cats with Oral Tumors
current_roster.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.


IACUC: 24619

Study number: VCCT-26-014


The study will provide $3000 toward initial diagnotic tests or radiation therapy for your pet.
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to characterize the clinical disease progression in dogs with glioma
current_roster.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma

current_roster.description: The VCC is currently enrolling cases in a nationwide clinical trial to evaluate a monoclonal antibody (AT-005) that is conditionally licensed by the USDA to aid in the treatment of dogs with lymphoma. The study is designed to assess the benefit of adding AT-005 to a multi-agent chemotherapy protocol for dogs with intermediate to high grade T-cell lymphoma. CLINICAL STUDY DETAILS Trial Summary An estimated 48 client-owned dogs will be enrolled in this study. All enrolled dogs will receive multiagent chemotherapy (CHOP protocol), which will be supplemented by either placebo or the monoclonal antibody. Dogs will be randomized equally (1:1) to receive antibody or placebo during the chemotherapy protocol and the veterinary oncologist performing the dog's evaluations will be blinded to their group assignment. Study visits are required twice weekly for four weeks, once weekly for another 15 weeks, and monthly thereafter. The study duration is 18 months; however, if progressive disease occurs before the 18-month visit, dogs will be removed from the study at that time. Trial Eligibility To qualify for enrollment, dogs must meet the following criteria: Client-owned dog > 1 year of age. Body weight at least 2 kg. Biopsy and flow cytometry confirmation of naive, intermediate or high grade T-cell lymphoma.Stage II or higher. At least one peripherally located lymph node measuring 2 cm longest diameter. Performance Score of 0, 1 or 2 "0 = normal activity; 1 = restricted activity: decreased activity from pre disease status; 2 = compromised, ambulatory only for vital activities, consistently defecates and urinates in acceptable areas" Dogs cannot be enrolled if any of the following conditions are met: Glucocorticoid therapy for more than 7 days prior to enrollment. Prior chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or molecular- targeted therapy. Any uncontrolled medical condition (including other concurrent malignancy) that may be disruptive to the intent and objectives of the study. Dog is pregnant or likely to become pregnant. Dog is participating in another study. Dog may not be available for the entire study duration
current_roster.name: Conditionally Licensed Monoclonal Antibody + multi-agent Chemotherapy for Dogs with T-Cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine the safety and efficacy of Aurolase therapy (nanoparticle infusion plus targeted laser treatment) in the treatment of canine and feline cancers Background Modern cancer therapies use strategies that aim to get rid of cancer while preserving healthy tissue and maintaining the best possible quality of life. The current treatments for dog and cat solid tumors include surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or any combination of these three. This study is investigating a gold nano-particle-based, ablative (removal) technique that aims to destroy tumor cells while limiting damage to healthy tissue. This approach has the potential to directly benefit animals with cancer, as well as indirectly benefit human cancer patients by advancing our knowledge of cancer therapy. Eligibility Pets with superficial or oral solid tumors 10cm LD or concurrent life threatening disease. Pets who have received chemotherapy within 3 weeks, or radiation within 6 months, prior to beginning the study. Pets with significant metastatic disease that would reduce the prognosis to <1 month if left untreated. Note: The Aurolase laser cannot penetrate bone, and therefore cannot be used to treat tumors that have spread to bone. Study Design After the initial pretreatment evaluation, pets will undergo two procedures. 1) Infusion with AuroShell Particles. This process is similar to chemotherapy administration. The nanoparticle infusion will last for 30-45 minutes. 2) Laser treatment of targeted tumor. This procedure will be carried out under general anesthesia. Laser dose will be delivered to the tumor site. Pets must return for follow-up visits at 3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 weeks post-treatment. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED
current_roster.name: Pilot Study of AuroLase® Therapy for the Treatment of Canine and Feline Solid Tumors

current_roster.description: AuroLase Therapy uses a therapeutic medical device designed to selectively destroy solid tumors using near infrared illumination from a laser. AuroLase Therapy is comprised of three components: 1) an off-the-shelf near infrared laser source, 2) an off-the-shelf interstitial fiber optic probe for delivery of the laser energy to a site near or inside the tumor, and 3) the investigational gold nanoparticles (AuroShell particles), a near infrared absorbing, physiologically inert material designed to absorb and convert laser energy into heat. Intravenously administered AuroShell particles have previously shown efficacy and high selectivity over surrounding healthy tissues in a variety of animal models. Human clinical trials are now progressing utilizing AuroLase Therapy for a number of clinical presentations and tumor types such as refractory head and neck, prostate, lung, and brain cancers. The purpose of the proposed study is to evaluate this therapy in dogs and cats with easily accessible spontaneous tumors. Dogs and cats will receive one AuroLase Therapy treatment and will then be followed for one month after treatment to observe anticancer activity and side effects. Dogs or cats that have been diagnosed with a malignant tumor that is easily accessible will be eligible for this study. Required study visits include pretreatment, day 0 (which may be the same day as pretreatment), day 1, 14, and 28. A physical examination and a small blood sample will be collected pretreatment, and days 1, 14, and 28. The AuroShell particles will be administered intravenously on study day 0. On study day 1 (approximately 24 hours after AuroShell particle infusion), your pet will be anesthetized for approximately 30 minutes for application of the laser treatment. While under anesthesia a tumor biopsy will be performed. Tumor biopsies will be repeated on study day 14 and 28 under mild sedation. Your pet may experience some local pain at the site of the biopsy and laser application. If this occurs, the clinician will prescribe pain medication. After study day 28 (or sooner if your pet is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional follow-up and treatment options with you. The study will cover all costs related to AuroLase Therapy treatment and required recheck examinations, blood tests and tumor biopsies. In addition, a gift of $250.00 will be applied as a credit to your UW Veterinary Care account.
current_roster.name: AuroLase Therapy for the Treatment of Solid Tumors in Cats and Dogs

current_roster.description: Injection site sarcomas (also known as a fibrosarcoma) are a rare tumor that can arise following injections in cats. While a specific cause is yet to be determined, there are treatments available such as the anti-cancer drug carboplatin. Drs.Kelly HumeandCheryl Balkmanof the oncology department are performinga study to determine if customized doses based on kidney function (rather than body weight) will be effective against the tumor. Initial visits can last anywhere from 6-8 hours but the owner is not required to remain in the hospital.A minimum of 2 additional follow-up visits are required, approximately 3 4 weeks apart. Weekly blood work monitoring in between these visits is required, but can be performed elsewhere. Owners will be responsible for the cost of monitoring/blood work not performed at Cornell.
current_roster.name: Refining Current Treatment for Cats with Injection Site Sarcomas

current_roster.description: 1.Purpose of the project The purpose of this project is to determine if AuroLase Therapy is feasible and safe to administer to canine and feline patients with spontaneously occurring tumors of the limbs and oral cavities. 2.Eligibility for participation Any treatment naive, recurrent, and/or refractor dog with a confirmed diagnosis of a soft tissue sarcoma or squamous cell carcinoma limited to the head and neck, oral cavity, or limb is eligible for enrollment. Any cat with a confirmed diagnosis of an oral squamous cell carcinoma that has not received treatment, has recurrent disease, or has not responded to treatment is eligible for enrollment. In addition, cats and dogs must be free from other pre-existing conditions which would make them poor candidates for treatment or anesthesia. For example, dogs with pre-existing heart, kidney, or liver disease may be ineligible for participation. 3.Expected duration of participation Study patients will receive one administration of AuroLase Therapy. The therapy will take place over 2 days, with treatment on day 1 taking approximately 30 to 60 minutes (dependent on the size of patient) and treatment on day 2 taking approximately 60 to 90 minutes (dependent on tumor size). Study patients will return home between the two treatment days. Study patients will be returned to their owners at the end of the second treatment day or stay at the Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital (VMTH) until ready for discharge. After AuroLase Therapy is completed; the study requires routine follow-up exams at the VMTH. Follow-up exams will occur 2 weeks after treatment and then once a month for 3 months. Each re-evaluation will take approximately 30 to 60 minutes. After 3 months, the patient's progress can be monitored either by the referring veterinarian or with the VMTH medical oncology service as part of routine cancer care.
current_roster.name: Thermal laser therapy for treatment of solid tumors in the extremities of canine and feline patients

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to find out how often cats with lymphoma are deficient in cobalamin (Vitamin B12). Additionally we are looking for a relationship between the level of cobalamin and methylmalonic acid (MMA) in the blood and the type of lymphoma, weight and body condition of the cat, as well as the change of weight over the first month of treatment. Cats who are presenting to the oncology service with a diagnosis of lymphoma who have not yet started treatment will be enrolled. Approximately 10 mL of blood will be taken from the cat. Each cat will be weighed and given a body condition score. If receiving treatment for lymphoma, we ask to be able to re-weigh and re-condition score the cat 4 weeks into treatment.
current_roster.name: Prevalence and Clinical Significance of Cobalamin Deficiency in Cats with Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a type of sarcoma that is difficult to treat because of its aggressive behavior and rapid progression after diagnosis. The first 21 dogs treated in the SRCBST study at the University of Minnesota showed that a bispecific targeted toxin (sarcoma bispecific targeted toxin, or SRCBST) is safe and doubles the expected survival time. SRCBST2 continues the research by Dr. Jaime Modiano, Dr. Antonella Borgatti and Dr. Michael Henson to determine the safest dose of SRCBST which is still effective. Results of this study will provide information to develop a therapy for both dogs and humans with this incurable disease. Dogs eligible for the study: 1. Diagnosed with HSA 2. Spleen removed by surgery either prior to study or at the Veterinary Medical Center 3. No evidence of metastasis (on chest x-ray, ultrasound) but if gross metastasis removed at time of splenectomy, may still be eligible 4. No concurrent kidney, liver or heart disease, or problems with blood clotting 5. No previous chemotherapy (prednisone is ok), cyclophosphamide, or alternative medications The study involves: PET-CT prior to start of treatment (optional but desired). This imaging will allow us to look for micro-metastasis but will not exclude dogs if any are found. PET-CT is performed under general anesthesia at a nearby University facility and requires an overnight stay following the procedure. Day 1, 3, 5 visit the VMC for SRCBST administration and follow up blood testing Day 8 chemotherapy begins, continues for total of 5 treatments, 3 weeks apart Day 21 - 2nd PET-CT (if first one was done and we saw no evidence of micro-metastasis Day 25-29: second round of SRCBST treatment, coincides with 2nd round of chemotherapy Day 88-92: Possible 3rd round of SRCBST at the time of the 5th chemotherapy, depending upon restaging results (bloodwork, X-ray, ultrasound) Month 6 follow up The owner is responsible for the initial oncology exam fee and staging diagnostics (approx $900-$1,100). If the dog is eligible, the study reimburses the owner for prescreening X-rays, ultrasound, bloodwork, urinalysis, then covers PET-CT and all study visits. The covered costs are equivalent to $8,500-$9,560 in value. In addition, the study covers up to $5,000 of chemotherapy treatment, which will be most if not all of the cost. Herbal medications such as Yunnan Bai Yao must be stopped prior to enrollment.
current_roster.name: SRCBST2: dose-finding for a ligand targeted toxin to treat hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: This is a University dog cancer trial using a new anti-cancer drug that is injected directly into cancers in the mouth. Participation requires 4 visits to the Veterinary Oncology Clinic at the University of Missouri in Columbia. Rationale: Locally invasive tumors are most often treated with surgery and radiation therapy. However, intratumoral delivery of chemotherapy drugs can achieve concentrations higher than would occur with intravenous or other routes of administration. This also delivers the drug directly to the tumor without significant drug exposure. This trial will evaluate a novel formulation of the drug cisplatin which is known to be effective against a wide variety of tumors. The nanoparticle formulation allows for better distribution through the tumor, uptake by cancer cells, and lymphatic trafficking to provide some chemotherapy to nearby lymph nodes that might be targets for metastatic cancer. 1.Purpose of Research The primary purpose of this study will be the evaluation of tolerability, collection of pharmacokinetic data, and tumor response as measured by RECIST criteria in dogs bearing naturally-occurring carcinomas (excluding anal sac adenocarcinomas) and melanoma. This clinical trial will refine the proper dosage for dogs with cancer and determine whether there is evidence of efficacy. 2.Expected Duration of Participation Dogs will be treated every 3 weeks for 4 treatments. At each treatment, NHA-cisplatin will be injected intra- and peri-tumoral. At the first treatment, each dog will stay in the hospital for a minimum of 24 hours to allow a total of 5 small blood samples to be collected over time to determine how the drug is metabolized. Dogs will need a blood (CBC, Mg, chemistry profile) and urine check one week after each chemotherapy treatment. 3.Description of Procedures Following complete staging, the tumor will be measured using the longest diameter, and this includes all target lesions. General anesthesia may be required for tumor measurement, and chemotherapy administration. Dogs will be evaluated every three weeks for tumor response until off trial. Abdominal ultrasound will be performed to evaluate tumor response if applicable tumor location. A complete blood count (CBC), magnesium and a chemistry panel will be required prior to each treatment and one week afterwards. Some dogs will be offered PET/CT scans to trace the chemotherapy at injection. For those dogs, a hospital stay of one night will be necessary after the scan for radiation isolation purposes. Dogs will be discharged from the hospital with specific instructions for handling post-scan. Please contact Debbie Tate @ tated@missouri.edu or call 573-882-7821 for more information.
current_roster.name: Phase I/II Evaluation of Cisplatin Hyaluronate Nanoparticles in Tumor-bearing Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study: Knowing whether or not there is metastatic tumor in the regional lymph nodes is very important prognostic information for dogs with lung tumors, as dogs that do not have metastatic disease in their lymph nodes in general have a much longer lifespan. Chemotherapy is often recommended for patients who have metastatic disease, but is not recommended for dogs who do not have metastatic spread. The aim of this study is to provide information that will allow us to better identify these lymph nodes at surgery, to improve the safety of surgical dissection, and to minimize surgical time during removal of these lymph nodes. Contact: Call 530-752-1393 and ask to speak to the Soft Tissue Surgery scheduling coordinators (Gigi, Conni, or Caleb) to schedule an appointment with Dr. Michele Steffey. Participation Requirements: A diagnosis of a solitary lung tumor Your decision to pursue surgical removal of your dogs lung tumor. Initial Evaluation for Participation: Evaluation by the V.M.T.H. Small Animal Surgery, Internal Medicine, or Oncology services. A CT scan at the VMTH is part of the normal expected surgical planning for lung tumor surgery at our institution, and is the financial responsibility of the client, but may be performed under the same anesthetic episode as the planned surgery. Dogs with severe kidney or liver disease are not eligible to participate. Procedures: During CT and surgery, special dyes will be injected intravenously or into the lung around your dog's tumor and uptake by the regional lymph nodes will be assessed. Benefits: Information regarding the status of your dog's lymph nodes is very important in prognosis for this disease. This technique will help surgeons to identify and more safely remove your dog's lymph nodes at surgery; pathology of the removed lymph node(s) will provide improved information to direct recommendations that we an give you for postoperative care and treatment. If based on the initial CT results you elect to have your dog go to surgery as part of this study, the study will retroactively pay for the cost of your dog's CT scan (a $900 value to you). Owner Responsibilities: There is no anticipated additional cost to you for your dog's participation in the study. The cost of the dyes and operative imaging are covered by the study. The primary risks of this procedure are 1) allergic reaction to the drugs used to identify the lymph nodes (very rare, but unpredictable in an individual patient (like any other drug reaction, including antibiotics)), and 2) air leakage from the lung at the site of the injection (if it occurs, this should be a short term problem, as removal of the affected lung will be performed as part of the tumor removal). If an allergic reaction should occur, immediate costs of treatment (immediate supportive medications, support of blood pressure) will be covered by the study; however, the owner will be responsible for any treatment costs for prolonged or severe complications. Standard anesthetic and surgical risks of lung surgery and lymph node surgery will apply and will be discussed at the time of your visit.
current_roster.name: Assessment of methods of improving identification of regional lymph nodes in patients with lung cancer

current_roster.description: Inclusion Criteria and General Background Information: Your dog must have a confirmed diagnosis of melanoma and several tests to ensure his/her general health and to assess how advanced the disease is prior to treatment. The tumor will be biopsied prior to therapy. Tumors must be large enough to biopsy and your dog must have no other significant health problems. Exclusion Criteria: Dogs with significant concurrent disease are excluded from this study. Dogs cannot be receiving concurrent chemotherapy (including corticosteroids) or radiation therapy. Dogs must be off of all such therapy for 3 weeks prior to study enrollment. No dogs under 15 kg (<33 lbs) will be allowed in this study. Owner Commitments: Prior to entry into this study, your dog must have a confirmed diagnosis of melanoma and staging tests to ensure his/her general health and to assess how advanced the disease is. The tumor will need to be biopsied before therapy for this purpose. Your dog will receive one of two drugs or a combination of the two. Both drugs are FDA approved and have been used in dogs previously for other reasons. Interactions between these drugs and other drugs are unknown; therefore it is important to tell your veterinarian about any medications (and supplements) your dog is currently taking. It is strongly encouraged to eliminate all unnecessary medications. This should be discussed with your oncologist if you have any questions. Financial Incentives: All costs associated with this study will be provided as part of your participation. In the event any complications arise during the twenty-nine (29) day study period (time period between drug administration and assessment), their management will be covered by study funds up to $1000/dog. This would include any unanticipated hospitalizations. However, all costs exceeding $1000/dog are your responsibility.
current_roster.name: Randomized trial comparing two treatments for malignant melanoma

current_roster.description: 1. Purpose of the project The primary objective of the study is to evaluate whether needle biopsy of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (those in the very back of the throat behind the nose) are valuable staging tests for dogs with head and neck tumors. 2. Eligibility for participation Dogs will be eligible to participate in the study if the presence of a head, neck or nasal tumor is confirmed via cytology or histopathology prior to the initiation of therapy and if they are undergoing advanced imaging (CT scan) of their tumor with evaluation of the lymph nodes for therapeutic planning as part of their normal diagnostic plan. 3. Expected duration of participation Dogs will participate on a one-time basis. Participation in this study will add approximately 10-15 min of anesthesia time to their normal imaging procedure. 4. Description of procedure Dogs will receive a CT scan, as part of their standard diagnostic or therapeutic work up, before participating in this procedure. After the imaging, dogs will be moved to the ultrasonography room where they will be placed on their backs in a soft padded trough while under anesthesia. The area under their chin will be shaved and cleanly prepped with alcohol. Using ultrasound guidance, a needle attached to a syringe will be placed through the skin and into the retropharyngeal lymph node. A sample of cells will be removed by applying suction and spread on a slide for review. There are two retropharyngeal lymph nodes and both will be sampled. After this sampling the dog will have concluded its involvement in the study and will be free to continue on with the therapeutic or diagnostic plan set forth with the senior clinician on the case. Any dog that is not tolerating anesthesia during the normal imaging procedure will be removed from the study. 5. Possible discomforts and risks Shaving may cause irritation to the skin (razor burn) that is very superficial but may be itchy and require topical medications. Additionally, hair may grow back in a different color. Needle aspirates of lymph nodes may cause bruising of the skin or underneath the skin (hematoma) that may take several days to resolve. This bruising is generally non-painful. Aspirates may also increase the size of the lymph nodes after the technique, which is why it is always done after the imaging scans. The extra anesthetic time is not expected to cause additional discomfort or risks to your dog, but with all anesthetic procedures, risks include respiratory and cardiac complications or even death. 6. Possible benefits of study Your dog may not receive any benefit from participation in the study. 7. Financial obligations and compensation or therapy for accidental injury or complications All costs associated with the needle biopsy will be covered by the study. Any other fees associated with imaging, anesthesia or the treatment of cancer will be the owner's responsibility.

current_roster.description: Purpose The purpose of this study is to compare the efficacy and safety of masitinib to placebo in the treatment of dogs with aggressive grade 2-3 non-resectable mast cell tumors, not previously treated by chemotherapy (other than corticosteroids) or radiotherapy. Masitinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that has been shown to improve long-term survival of dogs with non-resectable tumors. Background Mast cell tumors (MCT) in dogs are very common, accounting for approximately 20% of all skin tumors in dogs. They can arise from any skin site on the body, and while they often appear small and somewhat insignificant, they can be a very serious form of cancer in the dog. Some MCT's are easily removed without development of further problems; however, others may lead to a life-threatening disease if not properly identified and treated. Inclusion Criteria Dogs, any breed or sex, greater than 1 year of age and weighing more than 6.9 kg. Diagnosed with Patnaik grade 2 or 3, non-resectable, cutaneous mast cell tumor with or without regional lymph node involvement, with measurable lesion at inclusion (i.e., longest diameter 10 mm for cutaneous tumor or with short axis diameters 15 mm for lymph nodes). Non-resectable is defined as either: - medically non-resectable (margins would be unlikely free of tumor cells) or - non-resectable for the pet owner (e.g., amputation would be unacceptable to the owner). Dog with lesion accessible for biopsy. Adequate renal, hepatic and hematologic parameters - Absolute neutrophils count (ANC) 2000/mm3 - Platelets 100^109/L - Hemoglobin 10g/dL - Hematocrit 30% - AST/ALT 3 x ULN - Bilirubin 1.5 ULN - Albumin LLN - Creatinine ULN - BUN ULN - Urinary protein creatinine ratio (UPC) 1. Owner able and willing to comply with study visits and procedures per protocol. Owner able to understand, sign, and date consent form Exclusion Criteria Dogs previously treated by chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Dogs with subcutaneous tumors. Dogs with bone marrow involvement. Dogs with major surgery within 2 weeks of treatment initiation. Dogs with evidence of gastric bleeding. Dogs with any previous history of kidney disease or any previous known episode of proteinuria including post vaccinal. Dogs with other concomitant serious diseases (life expectancy less than 3 months). Lactating or pregnant bitch, dog intended for breeding. Dogs owned by staff associated with the study. Dogs with any GI disease associated with an active exudative enteropathy or past history of exudative enteropathy Previous treatment. Dogs treated with any investigational agent within 4 weeks prior to baseline for short-acting investigational agent, and within 12 weeks prior to baseline for long-acting investigational agent. Dogs with any vaccination within 4 weeks prior to baseline. Dogs treated with corticosteroids, within 3 weeks of treatment initiation Study Design The following screening tests will be performed in order to confirm your dog's eligibility: complete blood count, serum chemistry panel, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, fine needle aspiration of the spleen, bone marrow aspirate, tumor biopsy and c-kit mutation analysis If eligible, your dog will be randomized to receive a once daily oral dose of either masitinib or placebo. Your dog will return every 2 weeks for 24 weeks, then every 12 weeks thereafter if your dog has experienced a complete or partial response or stable disease after treatment. Standard blood work and urinalysis will be performed at each visit. Additional tests mey be performed at various points in the study, which include chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and fine needle aspiration. Prior studies of masitinib in dogs with mast cell tumors have identified potential side effects that may occur, which include vomiting and diarrhea. Medications will be provided to treat or prevent any study-related side effects. Client Incentive Free clinical staging. Free study medications. Free recheck exams
current_roster.name: DOUBLE-BLINDED STUDY TO COMPARE EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF MASITINIB TO PLACEBO IN THE TREATMENT OF GRADE II AND III NON-RESECTABLE MA

current_roster.description: The Morris Animal Foundation and the National Cancer Institute are sponsoring a clinical trial in dogs with newly diagnosed Osteosarcoma. This trial is being conducted by the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium. 180 dogs will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor and receive standard of care chemotherapy. Dogs will be randomized at time of enrollment to either receive standard of care alone or standard of care with orally administered rapamycin. Eligibility: Confirmed osteosarcoma diagnosis. Has not received any prior treatment for osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial In Dogs With Newly Diagnosed Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Nasal tumors are locally aggressive tumors of the nasal passages. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for dogs affected by this cancer. At the UW-VMTH, we have a TomoTherapy radiation delivery system, which targets radiation to the tumor while sparing the surrounding normal tissues from side effects. Stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) is the use of this very precise technology to deliver high doses of radiation in fewer treatments compared to conventional protocols. A conventional radiation protocol for nasal tumors involves 10 radiation treatments, given as one treatment per day for 10 days. To take advantage of the extreme accuracy of stereotactic radiation therapy, we are investigating the efficacy of a shorter protocol in which only 3 treatments are delivered over one week (on Monday, Wednesday and Friday). Compared to the conventional protocol, a higher dose of radiation is used for each treatment to achieve a similarly effective total dose. Potential benefits of stereotactic radiation therapy include fewer visits to the hospital for radiation treatments, fewer anesthetic events, and a lower risk of short-term side effects. We will assess the safety of this new approach by monitoring for any radiation-induced changes in the eye. Our hypothesis is that by delivering stereotactic radiation therapy, we will safely decrease the number of treatments needed to effectively treat nasal tumors in dogs. Dogs with a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of cancer affecting the nasal cavity (carcinoma or sarcoma), stages I-III may be eligible to participate in this study. Dogs with cribriform plate involvement and/or metastasis, or previous treatment for this cancer are not eligible. Dogs will be evaluated at 2 & 4 weeks and 3 & 6 months post-radiotherapy to assess tumor response and side effects, including ocular changes. Clients will receive financial compensation to cover the cost of their dog's follow-up evaluations, including scheduled hospital visits for a full examination including eye exams and a post-treatment CT scan.
current_roster.name: Stereotactic Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Nasal Tumors

current_roster.description: Radiation therapy's primary use for canine osteosarcoma has been with a palliative intent to alleviate pain. Stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT) is a highly accurate radiation delivery technique that potentially allows us to give a higher radiation dose per treatment in fewer treatment sessions. This study will deliver 3 radiation treatments over 3 days and assess pain relief with orthopedic exam, force platform analysis and client questionnaires. The primary aim of this study is to determine the effectiveness of stereotactic radiation therapy to alleviate pain. We hypothesize that most dogs will experience significant pain relief. Large doses of radiation per treatment have also been proposed to stimulate an immune response against the cancer. To evaluate this, we aim to measure changes in proteins released from the tumor or its environment by collecting blood samples before, during and after the radiation therapy. Two weeks following completion of the third radiation treatment, dogs will start intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy. Carboplatin will be administered once every 3 weeks for a total of 4 treatments. Dogs with a biopsy confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma of the limb may be eligible for this study. Dogs with a tumor-related fracture, spread of cancer to lymph nodes or lungs or previous radiation or chemotherapy are not eligible. A CT scan will be required for radiation planning and to determine study eligibility. Dogs will be evaluated at 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 and 14 weeks after radiation therapy. Clients will receive financial compensation, which will cover the cost of radiation therapy and follow-up evaluations. Clients are responsible for the cost of diagnosis and tests to determine if their dog is eligible for this study and for the carboplatin chemotherapy.
current_roster.name: Stereotactic Radiation Therapy for Pain Relief and Immune Modification in Dogs with Limb Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Work at the Cork Cancer Research Center in Ireland has lead to the development of a novel new energy based therapy for treating inoperable human cancers including those unresponsive to conventional chemo and radiotherapy. Since 2004 over 400 energy focused cancer treatments have been provided to patients with unresponsive skin based cancers at the Mercy University Hospital, Cork. Over 85% of the tumors treated have been reduced in size by more than 50% after one treatment. The treatment involves the application of a brief electrical pulse (under local anesthetic in people) directly to the tumor tissue. This causes the tumor cells to become temporarily porous and results in a significant increase in the tumor cells absorption of the chemotherapeutic drug. This treatment is extremely suitable for animals particularly in cases where the cancer is considered inoperable. In animals, the device is attached to an existing endoscope and during a standard endoscopic procedure the tumor is enveloped (sometimes in several locations due to tumor size) and treated after IV administration of chemotherapy with the intent that circulating chemotherapy will drive into the open cancer cells, effectively killing them. For intra-operative locations, the device may be placed directly onto the tumor with surgical access if necessary. A newer device is now available to treat tumors using thoracoscopy or laparoscopy as minimally invasive options. Tumors that may respond include colon tumors, stomach, esophageal, prostate, adrenal and other non-resectable cancers. Frequently Asked Questions: 1) Will this therapy cure the cancer? The therapy is effective at the location where the electrodes are placed on the animal i.e. the visible tumor mass; provided contact can be made endoscopically the tumor mass can be reduced if not eliminated with minimal side effects 2) How long does the treatment take? The procedure is completed under anesthesia (isoflurane/sevoflurane). Injection of a low dose of chemotherapy (the total is 5% of what would be used conventionally) and application of electrodes directly to the tumor with pulses used taking less than 1/10th of a second to deliver. The pet is treated and able to go home the same day. 3) What chemotherapy drug is used? Is the chemotherapy toxic? The drug used in combination with the electric pulses is Bleomycin. On its own, bleomycin is very poorly absorbed by cells and is considered a poor drug for the treatment of cancer. However, by making the tumor cells porous (because they receive an electrical pulse), the drug can enter locally (but not to other cells in the body), and this results in the tumor cells dying. It also means that the toxicity is limited to the site of where the electrodes are placed which means side effects are truly unlikely. 4) Will my pet lose its hair from the chemo? No. A very low concentration of drug is used and is only toxic at the location the electrodes are placed i.e. on the tumor tissue. 5) Does anesthetic need to be used? Will my pet feel pain or discomfort? Human patients who receive local anesthetic feel the electric pulse and have described it as a dull thud. The anticipation is apparently worse than the discomfort of the pulse which it is important to point out subsides virtually immediately (the pulse lasts 1/10th of a second). In animals, the easiest solution is general anesthetic (isoflurane/sevoflurane) normally for between 15-30mins in total. In this case no discomfort is felt by the pet. 6) Is it an invasive treatment, does it involve surgery and stitches afterward? Unless surgery is needed to approach the tumor, no surgery is involved and therefore the therapy does not involve stitches. For extremely large tumors that are operable a possible combination treatment is to deliver the treatment to the healthy tissue margins afterward to minimize the risk of residual cancer cells escaping. 7) What side effects does the treatment have? No side effects have been reported from the drug or the electric pulses in humans. Some inflammation may occur in larger tumors but this can easily be managed with medication or with many cases subsides without additional therapy needed. 8) What should happen after treatment? How long will it take to see a response? The tumor is not surgically removed; it shrinks and regresses in size over a period of a few weeks after treatment. The speed at which this happens can vary depending on the type and size of the tumor. Normally a reduction in size can be seen within 2 weeks and regression can continue for up to 2 months. Aggressive cancers can be retreated after 4-6 weeks to improve the speed of regression. 9) Which patients are best for treatment? Any animal with a solid tumor can be treated. Dogs, Cats, and Horses have all been treated successfully. 10) Which cancers are best for treatment? Any solid tumor can be treated. Those located on the skin are the most straightforward to identify, diagnose and treat. Internal cancers can be treated during open surgery or via this specially designed endoscopic/internal equipment developed at the Cork Cancer Research Center. Particularly suited are those cancers considered inoperable or that involve invasive surgery e.g. to the head, legs or internal organs. current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: It is known that a specific protein in the membrane of the nucleus, XP01, controls the shuttling of several key proteins in and out of the nucleus (center) of the cell. Recent studies indicate that blocking XP01 can induce death of cancer cells as they cannot recover function when the shuttling of proteins is disrupted; in contrast, normal cells appear to be less sensitive to this effect, likely because they are not growing in an uncontrolled manner. The novel compound Verdinexor is an inhibitor of XP01 that is given orally twice per week. Verdinexor has been studied in 2 separate clinical trials in dogs with lymphoma with over 75 dogs treated to date. Approximately 30-40% of dogs with both newly diagnosed and relapsed lymphoma appear to benefit from Verdinexor treatment staying on therapy for over 8 weeks. The main side effect of Verdinexor is loss of appetite and weight loss, with other side effect such as intestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea) and liver value elevations occurring less frequently. RV1001 is a novel inhibitor of a cell protein called PI3K delta. This drug, like verdinexor, is given orally. PI3Kdelta has an important role in both T and B cells, providing signals for cell survival. Recently, RV1001 was evaluated in a clinical trial of dogs with both T and B cell lymphoma. The overall objective response rate was 62% (3 complete and 10 partial responses) demonstrating very high biologic activity. Increases in liver enzymes were the primary side effect observed, and this was prevented in most dogs by giving the drug Monday through Friday with the weekends off, rather than daily without a break. While the activity of RV1001 was very high, the average time on drug was only 4 weeks indicating that the dogs rapidly developed resistance. Given the potential for both RV1001 and verdinexor to have activity in dogs with lymphoma and the non-overlapping side effects of each drug, the purpose of this study is to evaluate the effects of both drugs in combination. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity when verdinexor is administered in combination with RV1001 in dogs with lymphoma, and to assess the clinical toxicities in dogs with lymphoma receiving verdinexor in combination with RV1001.

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) is a chaperone protein that is important in maintenance of several proteins needed to promote cancer cell growth and survival. Hsp90 activity has been shown to be increased in cancer cells. Hsp90 inhibitor drug conjugates (HDCs) are small molecules that link an anti-cancer drug to an Hsp90 inhibitor. The Hsp90 inhibitor helps bring the anti-cancer drug inside the cancer cells. The anti-cancer drug can then be slowly released inside the cancer cells. Synta Pharmaceuticals has developed STA-12-8960, an Hsp90 inhibitor linked to SN-38, an active metabolite of the anti-cancer (chemotherapy) drug irinotecan. A recently completed clinical trial in dogs with cancer identified a dose of 15 mg/kg given intravenously weekly as the maximum tolerated dose. In this study, several responses to therapy were noted including dogs with lymphoma and mast cell tumors. Side effects were mild in most dogs and consisted of appetite loss and diarrhea, although these were well controlled with additional medications. Objective of the trial: The objective of this study is to compare the plasma and intratumoral concentrations of SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma receiving first irinotecan followed by STA-12-8960 to determine whether STA-12-8960 does result in greater intratumoral drug concentrations.

current_roster.description: The study will test whether an adenovirus based vaccine followed by a DNA plasmid administered via electrogenetransfer can elicit anti-tumor immunity and increase survival times. Most dogs undergo amputation and chemotherapy for bone cancer with median survival of about 1 year due to metastatic spread to the lungs. The vaccine will be an additional therapy to standard of care treatment. Up to 60% of dogs with osteosarcoma will express the Her2/neu genetic marker. Telomerase and HER-2/neu as targets of genetic cancer vaccines in dogs. Peruzzi D, Mesiti G, Ciliberto G, La Monica N, Aurisicchio L. Vaccine. 2010 Feb 3;28(5):1201-8. Epub 2009 Nov 26. The vaccine targets this Her2/neu pathway of tumorigenesis allowing the body's immune system to battle the cancer in addition to standard therapies. PROCEDURE: Vaccine is a series of 5 treatments (2 adenovirus/Her2/neu) followed by 3 DNA/plasmid administered via electrogenetherapy (EGT). Each is administered every 2 weeks and there is an option for continued monthly boosters for those patients maintaining remission. The first two (2) adenovirus vaccines (prime) are administered via simple intra-muscular injection. The last three (3) of the series (boosters) are administered under a short anesthesia via EGT. No placebos are involved and the study is unfunded and under USDA regulations. This immunotherapy is an extension of the center's telomerase cancer vaccine that has shown success against canine lymphoma in Europe. There is no guarantee and some patients may not benefit.
