current_roster.description: 20 dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor followed by standard of care chemotherapy. Once standard of care chemotherapy is completed, 10 of the dogs will receive an additional investigational chemotherapy agent.
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial in Dogs with Newly Diagnosed Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Background: There are many cases of malignant tumors in dogs that are not amenable to conventional therapeutic approaches, such as surgery, because of their location on the body or their advanced stage of disease. For such patients, therapeutic options are limited, because intravenous systemic chemotherapy may not be tolerable for these patients in their debilitated state, or perhaps it does not seem practical to put such patients through a prolonged radiation protocol away from their owners and home. The primary purpose of this study, therefore, is to demonstrate the feasibility and safety of a therapeutic protocol that may prove clinically beneficial in that subset of patients with externally-measurable malignant tumors, that are not amenable to surgery for whatever reason. This therapeutic protocol incorporates the localized intratumoral (subcutaneous) administration of a nanoparticle formulation of hyaluronan conjugated cisplatin (HA-Pt) in combination with palliative radiation therapy. Clinical Protocol: All enrolled dogs will receive HA-Pt subcutaneously to the primary tumor on study days 0, 7, 14, and 21, at incrementally increasing doses. Within 4 hours of HA-Pt administration, enrolled dogs will also concurrently receive one fraction of radiation therapy to the tumor site (for a total of 4 factions). Blood samples will be collected immediately prior to each dose of HA-Pt and also weekly for three weeks following the final dose. After study day 42 (or sooner if your dog is removed from the study), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional treatment options with you.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of hyaluronan conjugated cisplatin localized nanoparticle therapy combined with palliative radiation therapy in dogs wi

current_roster.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Mast cell tumors are the most common skin tumor in dogs, comprising between 16 and 21% of all canine malignant skin cancers. The currently accepted approach to therapy for high grade mast cell tumors is surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, or other adjuvant therapy. You, the owner of a dog with a suspected mast cell tumor (MCT) have already elected surgical excision of your dogs tumor. This study is specifically focused on the generation and characterization of a panel of cell lines established from canine mast cell tumor tissues. Your participation in this study is only to donate your dogs tumor tissue to a panel of other MCTs for further research. This panel of canine mast cell tumor cell lines will then be utilized by researchers for future investigations into mast cell-mediated disorders, specifically for the development of enhanced diagnostic, monitoring and treatment approaches for canine mast cell tumors. These canine mast cell tumor-derived cell lines will also be crucial to translational research by helping to further elucidate human mast cell neoplasia, and other human and canine diseases characterized by mast cell-mediated immune dysregulation. Clinical Protocol: This study involves only the staging of the mast cell tumor disease and the use of the resected tumor tissue in in vitro research. Owners of dogs diagnosed with a suspected mast cell tumor that have already elected to have the tumor surgically removed, will be agreeing to donate their dogs tumor tissue to this study.
current_roster.name: Characterization of canine mast cell tumors and generation of primary cell lines.

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to evaluate the clinical and immunologic activity of Immunolight Therapy (IT) in dogs with spontaneously-occurring solid tumors. The effect of IT on locally treated solid tumors will be measured via tumor size reduction (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; RECIST). The effect of IT on pulmonary metastatic lesion will be assessed via serial thoracic radiography. Changes in local, regional, and systemic immune activity will be measured via flow cytometry of tumor, regional lymph node and distant lymph node samples, for lymphoid and myeloid markers, as well as PD-1 expression. The effect of localized IT treatment of 2 lymphomatous lymph nodes on systemic disease burden will be measured through a combination of lymph node size reduction (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; RECIST), radiographic assessment of thoracic lesions, and cytologic assessment of previously affected nodes.Safety will also be assessed; all clinical and biochemical toxicities will be graded according to the Veterinary Comparative Oncology Group Common Terminology criteria for Adverse Events (VCOG-CTCAE) v1.1 (Veterinary Comparative Oncology, 2011).
current_roster.name: Clinical Trials of Immunolight Therapy for Pet Dogs with Cancer

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Despite surgery and chemotherapy treatment, most dogs develop metastatic disease (spread) to the lungs, which is ultimately their cause of death. Zoledronate is a drug used to treat osteoporosis, as well as bony metastases in humans. It has also been used in dogs with bone tumors to relieve pain. It may also have anti-tumor effects, and there are some reports of stable or improved disease in people with lung metastases. This trial is investigating the use of zoledronate in dogs with pulmonary metastatic disease.
current_roster.name: Drug treatment for dogs with lung involvement of bone cancer

current_roster.description: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma is a rare form of lymphoma where cancerous lymphocytes localize to the skin or mucocutaneous sites (i.e. gums). Dogs typically present with multiple lesions spread over the body, inhibiting the use of local therapies such as surgery or radiation therapy. This disease tends to be responsive to chemotherapy; however, the duration of response to our standard protocols is typically short. Lomustine is an oral chemotherapeutic drug commonly used for cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). While the majority of dogs treated for CTCL with lomustine will improve, only around 30% of dogs will achieve a complete remission from this drug alone. Combination chemotherapy protocols are the gold standard of treatment for other forms of canine lymphoma. These protocols have been shown to not only have the highest remission rates, but also the longest remission durations. The goal of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of combining lomustine with another chemotherapeutic agent, asparaginase, specifically for dogs with CTCL.
current_roster.name: Combined Lomustine and Asaparaginase for Treatment of Canine Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Regulatory T-cells (Tregs)are immune cells that have been found to be increased in humans and dogs with cancer. The immune system of cancer-bearing cats has not been evaluated. This study aims to assess the numbers of Tregs in three populations of cats: those with lymphoma, those with carcinomas, and those with sarcomas.
current_roster.name: Assessment of immune cells in cats with cancer

current_roster.description: This clinical trial seeks dogs with osteosarcoma to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a new vaccine following standard of care therapy. Bone cancer or osteosarcoma (OSA) is a common, highly aggressive cancer that frequently affects the long bones of large breed dogs. Current standard of care therapy consists of surgical limb amputation plus 4 doses of chemotherapy, given in a vein, every 3 weeks. The immune system plays an important role in identifying and targeting cancer cells in the body. In this study, we aim to use a new approach to stimulate the bodys own immune system to attack remaining tumor cells in dogs that have undergone limb amputation and chemotherapy for the treatment of OSA. We will use a study vaccine, which has been modified to express a tumor protein (HER-2/neu) that is found in many cancer cells, including canine bone cancer cells and cancer stem cells. The hope is that when injected into the bloodstream, the vaccine stimulates the immune system to attack cells expressing the HER-2/neu tumor protein. This approach aims to delay and/or prevent the spread of cancer (metastases) following removal of the primary bone cancer tumor (limb amputation) and chemotherapy. Interactions with other drugs are unknown, so it is necessary to disclose any medications (and supplements) your dog is currently taking to the oncologist. It is strongly encouraged to eliminate all unnecessary medications. **Please note that all staging diagnostics (including but not limited to radiographs, ultrasound, and blood work) must be performed at Cornell University prior to surgery and chemotherapy. Full amputation surgery must also be performed at Cornell within 10 days of the initial staging diagnostics. Following surgery all chemotherapy and vaccine administration appointments must also be performed at Cornell. Please contact the clinical trials coordinator for more information.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a Vaccine for the Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: A new combination of drugs (ibrutinib + mivibresib) will be tested in a phase II clinical study in untreated dogs that have been newly diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma at both Cornell University Hospital for Animals and Cornell University Veterinary Specialists. After owner consent, a peripheral lymph node excision will be performed prior to treatment, and for all dogs, a fine needle aspiration will be performed in an involved node, both before and at 2 and 4 weeks after study initiation, if palpable tumor remains. Serum and blood for germline DNA will be collected prior to treatment and at remission or at 4 weeks, whichever is later. Dogs will be followed every week for the first four-week cycle and every four weeks after that. Treatment will continue until progression or for six cycles, whichever comes first. Doses in the only reported study with ibrutinib in canine B-cell lymphoma ranged from 2 to 20 mg/kg, responses were seen at all concentrations, and the receptor occupancy was 100% for 24 hours at all dose levels. For this study, we chose a dose of 5mg/kg as a tolerable dose in the lower end of this range that was similar to the ~8mg/kg used in human studies. Mivibresib dose was recommended based on PK studies done by Abbvie (0.1 mg/kg/day). To ensure safety in the clinical trial, the starting dose of ibrutinib will be held constant at 5mg/kg and the dose of Mivibresib will be reduced by 50% in the first four dogs treated with each combination to ensure that dogs with lymphoma respond similarly to healthy research beagles. If no dose limiting toxicities are encountered after one cycle of treatment, the dose of Mivibresib will be increased to 100%, and subsequent dogs will be treated at 5mg/kg ibrutinib + full dose of Mivibresib. If toxicity occurs at any cycle of treatment, dose adjustments will be made first to Mivibresib (reduce dose by 25-50% at the discretion of the treating oncologist), and then to ibrutinib (reduce dose to 2.5mg/kg) if side effects still persist at a 50% dose reduction of the partner agent. If side effects persist after these dose reductions, the patient will be removed from the study.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a New Drug Combination to Treat Lymphoma

visible_sc_items.label: Medication costs included, other costs go to owner

current_roster.description: Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are tumors that arise from various skin and connective tissues under the skin, such as fat, muscle, cartilage, nerves, or small blood vessels. These tumors can occur from any site on the body and commonly regrow after tumor removal. While surgical removal and other therapies are available to treat these tumors, little is known as to why the occur in the first place. Dr. Andrew Miller and his lab are collecting samples of canine soft tissue sarcomas in order to determine their RNA molecules, otherwise known as transcriptome. This information will one day lead to new treatments and preventives for these tumors.
current_roster.name: Determining the Transcriptome of Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma

current_roster.description: PetCure Oncology, in collaboration with Varian Medical Systems, is currently accepting animals into a clinical trial to study the immune response of dogs that receive stereotactic radiation (SRS/SRT) to treat osteosarcoma, oral malignant melanoma, sino-nasal tumors, or thyroid carcinoma. All four of these tumor types are known to have the potential to spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body. This clinical trial was launched to evaluate specific immune cells found in the blood. These immune cells have been found to impact survival in people across several tumor types that also have metastatic potential. Early data collected by PetCure Oncology as well as other investigators suggests that SRS/SRT in dogs may have a positive effect on the immune cells responsible for attacking cancer, leading to longer survival times than a traditional treatment course centered around surgical tumor removal including amputation. One hypothesis for this is that SRS/SRT not only treats the primary tumor, but it may also modulate the anti-tumor immune response in a manner that inhibits the spread of the cancer. The purpose of this trial is to test this theory. Enrollment in this trial is for dogs undergoing SRS/SRT for treatment of qualified cases of osteosarcoma, oral malignant melanoma, sinus/nasal tumors, or thyroid carcinoma. It involves participation in four (4) scheduled blood draws extending 1-month post-treatment. All trial-related blood draws will be free of charge, and pet owners will be provided $2,000 in compensation towards their treatment. If you are the owner or veterinarian of a dog with diagnosed or suspected osteosarcoma, oral malignant melanoma, sinus/nasal tumors, or thyroid carcinoma, contact ClinicalTrials@PetCureOncology.com or call 833-PET-HERO for additional details.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of the Systemic Immune Effects of Stereotactic Radiation (SRS/SRT) in Osteosarcoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma, Sino-Nasal

current_roster.description: This study is designed to collect additional safety data for Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector (AT-014), which is conditionally licensed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Dogs must have undergone amputation of the affected limb and have completed chemotherapy prior to entering the study. Not all sites are currently enrolling patients. Please contact sites directly to determine eligibility and timing of possible enrollment.
current_roster.name: Additional Field Safety Testing of Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector

current_roster.description: Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. Most dogs with TCC initially show signs such as straining to urinate, increased frequency of urination, or blood in the urine. As the tumor grows, it obstructs the flow of urine, which can become life-threatening. TCC can also spread to nearby lymph nodes, lungs, and bones. In most cases, TCC of the bladder cannot be cured. Common treatment options include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), chemotherapy, stent placement, or radiation therapy. Most dogs with TCC of the bladder succumb to their cancer within 6 to 8 months of diagnosis. Recently, a tumor protein called V600E B-Raf has been identified in up to 87% of dogs with TCC. This clinical trial is evaluating a bacterial vaccine that encourages the immune system to target the V600E B-Raf protein. We aim to determine if this vaccine is safe, and if it can delay tumor growth or spread and extend survival in dogs with TCC.
current_roster.name: TRANSITIONAL CELL CARCINOMA - Clinical Trial Using Immunotherapy For Female Dogs With Bladder Cancer

current_roster.description: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of new formulation of an old chemotherapy drug called paclitaxel in dogs with mast cell or solid tumors. Paclitaxel is not water soluble and therefore needs to be formulated with a chemical that permits intravenous administration. Unfortunately, the chemical (cremephor) causes allergic reactions and limits the ability to use this drug in dogs. A new water soluble formulation of paclitaxel was developed (Paccal Vet) and tested in dogs with mast cell tumors, mammary tumors and oral squamous cell carcinoma tumors. While there were some responses to therapy, drug administration was limited by side effects to the bone marrow, primarily low white blood cell count. ART207 is a new formulation of paclitaxel in which the drug is encapsulated in a lipid (fat) protein complex designed to promote specific uptake of the complexes through cholesterol receptors that are expressed in tumors. An ongoing safety study in normal healthy dogs demonstrated that ART207 can be administered at doses over twice those used in the Paccal Vet study, with no side effects to the bone marrow. Therefore, the ART207 results in much higher exposures to paclitaxel than the previous formulations and may have greater anti-tumor activity in dogs with cancer. This will be an open label clinical trial in which all dogs will receive ART 207 every 21 days. Dogs with cutaneous mast cell tumors or solid tumorsare eligible to enroll. These dogs may have failed conventional therapy or the owners may not desire to pursue conventional therapy at this time. Dogs will receive ART 207 IV on an anticipated schedule of every 21 days for a total of 4 treatments. Response to therapy will be assessed 21 days after each treatment and ART 207 administration will continue in the setting of stable disease or partial/complete response to therapy. Those dogs with progressive disease will be removed from the study. Analysis of dogs for tumor response will be performed by caliper measurement of the tumor and photographic documentation. Standard clinical chemistries (CBC, chemistry panel, and urinalysis) will be performed during the study. Additionally, 24-hour pharmacokinetic analyses will be performed following the first dose of ART 207, and plasma will be collected at each study visit to assess basal paclitaxel plasma concentrations at each study visit.
current_roster.name: Phase 1 study of ART 207 in dogs with solid tumors
current_roster.top_investigator: Cheryl London, D.V.M., Ph.D., DACVIM (Oncology), Professor in Comparative Oncology

current_roster.description: When a person or dog is diagnosed with cancer it is important to determine if the disease has spread throughout the body. This is called staging. Head and neck tumors usually go first to the local lymph nodes. Presently the only way to be sure if the cancer has spread there is to surgically remove the lymph nodes and look at them under the microscope. Imaging with CT or ultrasound can help, but is often not a very accurate way to tell if the cancer has metastasized. Iron nanoparticles (trade marked as a product called Feraheme) are taken up by normal cells in a lymph node. When cancer has infiltrated the lymph node there is no uptake. This can be visualized on MRI and in people has been shown to be a remarkably sensitive way to look for metastasis. The goal of this study is to determine if this novel, non-invasive imaging method utilizing iron nanoparticles is more sensitive than other types of imaging for diagnosing metastatic lymph nodes. On the first day of the study, dogs will receive an intravenous infusion of a medication called Ferumoxytol. This will be mixed with saline and given over 15-20 minutes after which we will monitor the dogs for any potential side effects. 48 hours later a CT and MRI will be performed. Dogs will then have several lymph nodes surgically excised so that they can be examined for presence of metastatic disease. Results from this test will be compared with the results of the imaging findings.
current_roster.name: LNMRI for Diagnosing Metastatic Lymph Nodes

current_roster.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that a certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib (PalladiaTM) is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib as well. In addition, we have discovered that the angiotensin receptor blocking (ARB) drug losartan also functions to block monocyte activity. In recent studies, we have also determined that treatment with the combination of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as toceranib, together with losartan exerts significantly greater antitumor activity than either drug alone. In addition, a clinical trial recently completed of high-dose losartan plus toceranib in dogs with metastatic OS demonstrated an overall biologic response rate of 50% and a measureable response rate of 30%, with acceptable toxicity. Thus, there is reason to expect that the combination will be well-tolerated and active in dogs with metastatic OS in this second clinical trial.
current_roster.name: Palladia and High Dose Losartan in Dogs with Metastatic Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: We are recruiting dogs with osteosarcoma (OSA) of the appendicular skeleton to assess the effectiveness of cryoablation and an investigational immunotherapy (STING agonist) to treat this disease. Cryoablation is a technique to freeze tumors that may kill the tumor, alleviate pain, and assist the body in rejecting cancer that has spread. During participation in this study, dogs will have a chest CT scan will be obtained to assess the presence of metastatic disease. Immediately prior to cryotherapy or STING agonist treatment, blood and an MR-guided or CT-guided tumor biopsy will be performed. Dogs receiving STING agonist alone or in combination with cryotherapy will received one dose of STING agonist in the tumor at the time of biopsy. A second dose of STING agonist will be given approximately one week later. All treatments will be performed under general anesthesia or sedation. Following cryoablation +/- immunotherapy, it is recommended that dogs undergo amputation (or limb sparing surgical excision) at two weeks after cryoablation followed by chemotherapy. Serial MR and CT imaging and blood sampling will be performed at intervals every 3 months after cryoablation.
current_roster.name: Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial in Dogs

current_roster.description: To assess the effectiveness of Y-90 endovascular radiosurgery in slowing or reversing the progression of caninehypervascularbrain tumors. Y-90 endovascular surgery is a minimally invasive, targeted injection of Yttrium-90-loaded microspheres into the blood vessels of a tumor under X-ray guidance.
current_roster.name: Therapy for Dogs with Brain Cancer

current_roster.description: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up.
current_roster.name: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: While conventional chemotherapy can induce remission in many dogs with lymphoma, relapse almost always occurs, and dogs with T cell lymphoma tend to have outcomes that are worse than average. Novel therapies for lymphoma, especially T cell lymphoma, are needed. CP-818 inhibits a novel cellular pathway that has been shown to induce cell death in some T cell lymphoma cells. Inhibitors of this pathway hold great promise for treating T cell lymphoma, and unpublished work suggests that a combination of CP-818 and the conventional chemotherapy drug doxorubicin are significantly more effective than either drug alone. CP-818 has been tested in rats at doses 10 times higher than the doses we plan to use, and in normal healthy dogs at the approximate dose we plan to use, without evidence of any adverse effects. CP-818 has been given to dogs with cancer and appears well tolerated. The dose of doxorubicin we are using has been used in dogs with cancer for decades, and has an acceptable and predictable likelihood of adverse effects. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this combination given to dogs with T cell lymphoma that have not yet been treated. Your dog will receive CP-818 orally twice daily, and will receive a conventional dose of doxorubicin once every 3 weeks for up to 5 treatments. He/she will be rechecked weekly for the first 4 weeks, then every third week thereafter. Visits where doxorubicin is given will generally take about 4 hours. He/she will be eligible to continue receiving treatment at no cost as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include blood draws and 2 or 3 biopsies of the lymph nodes over the course of the study to determine how CP-818 is affecting the cancer cells. These biopsies will be performed using standard sedation/anesthesia protocols, the biopsy site will be sutured, and sutures removed 2 weeks later. The visits when biopsies are performed may require a longer time, approximately half a day. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 9 teaspoons. Slightly more will be collected on Days 7 and 14 to measure the amounts of drug in the blood following treatment.
current_roster.name: Preclinical Evaluation Of Combined CP-818 And Doxorubicin For Treatment Of Canine Multicentric T Cell Lymphoma

current_roster.description: This is a multi-institutional consortium including UAB and veterinary colleges using an innovative immunotherapeutic approach to treating malignant glial brain tumors in pet dogs. Pet dogs share their environment (and oftentimes even their diet) with their owners. Dogs and humans develop sporadic benign and malignant brain tumors at about the same rate and with similar histopathology. Dogs are often euthanized due to the cost of care. Thus, the spontaneously occurring canine brain tumor represents an ideal opportunity to improve the lives of people and pets through comparative oncology and genomics and the One Medicine approach to research and direct clinical application. Malignant gliomas are the most common primary brain tumors in humans, accounting for 30% of all primary central nervous system (CNS) tumors in adults. With few major advances in decades, there has been no significant reduction in mortality and only a modest improvement in median survival. Recently, objective responses and long-term survivals have been observed in human glioma patients who have received oncolytic virotherapy and a Phase I trial is currently underway at UAB in patients using M032 alone. In this way, the human can served as a model for translation to the pet dog with malignant glioma. Following surgery to remove all or part of the tumor, a clinical grade oncolytic herpes simplex virus that expresses human interleukin-12 (currently being used in the concurrent human trial) will be injected into the resected tumor bed. Some dogs will also receive a drug called a checkpoint inhibitor. The dog is an ideal large animal model for diagnostic and therapeutic studies and can be used to translate successes to human patients while providing compassionate care to animals and advancing the field of veterinary medicine. These studies are designed to address key issues of safety and efficacy of combination immunotherapy in the dog that can be translated to humans with malignant gliomas.
current_roster.name: "CANINE": Brain Tumor Trial

current_roster.description: When a dog has been diagnosed with osteosarcoma (an aggressive bone tumor often found in the leg bones) removal of the primary tumor is commonly recommended. After removal (which in a lot of cases means amputation of the affected limb) the bone can be examined to look for several factors that may affect your pets survival. One factor that has been showed to be potentially prognostic is the presence of a type of cell called a tumor associated macrophage (TAM). This study is trying to develop a noninvasive way to determine how many of these cells are present in a bone tumor. The hope is that in future we can calculate TAM concentration prior to amputation. On the first day of the study you pet will be placed under anesthesia for imaging. Initially we will do an MRI of your pets leg that will take approximately 30-45 minutes. Following recovery from anesthesia your pet will receive an intravenous infusion of a medication called ferumoxytol. This will be mixed with saline and given over 15-20 minutes after which we will monitor him/her for any potential side effects. 36-48 hours later a repeat MRI will be performed just before the surgical amputation of the affected limb. The bone will then be sent for histology which will help us determine how many TAMs are present in the tumor.
current_roster.name: Ultra-Small Paramagnetic Iron Oxide Particle MRI for Imaging Appendicular Canine Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Electrochemotherapy is the ability to target the cancer by using an electrical impulse to open the cell membrane driving chemotherapy to the site (www.vetelectrochemotherapy.com). The electrode is equivalent to 14 F urinary catheter and is inserted retrograde under anesthesia. After treatment, a standard urinary catheter is placed and the patient remains hospitalized in the ICU for 1-2 days. Treatment may be single or 2-3 times over 2-4 months.
current_roster.name: Electrochemotherapy (ECT) to Treat Urethral Cancer

current_roster.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of CB-5339, a novel anticancer agent, when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently planned human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. The goal of this study is to establish the safety, tolerability, and maximally tolerated dose of oral CB-5339 when administered daily for 4 days a week for 2 weeks, with one week off, to dogs with various types of cancer. Prior to starting treatment, dogs will have a tumor biopsy and bone marrow aspirate performed for study purposes. The study drug will be given orally in 21-day cycles: 4 days per week for two weeks and one week off. After the first dose of treatment, dogs will need to stay in the hospital for the day for serial blood collections and tumor biopsies, and return the following day for blood collection and tumor biopsy. Recheck visits will be required on Days 8, 15, and 22 of the study for a physical exam and blood collection. A tumor biopsy will also be done on Day 8. If the dog is responding to treatment, he or she can continue on the study for additional treatment cycles.
current_roster.name: COTC028: Preclinical Assessment of an oral p97 inhibitor, CB-5339, in Tumor-Bearing Dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine whether giving ALT-803 (a cytokine interleukin-15 superagonist) will be safe and effective for treating cancer that has spread to the lungs. The hypothesis is that subcutaneous administration of ALT-803 in cancer-bearing dogs will mobilize and activate immune cells including Natural Killer and memory T cells, translating to favorable anti-tumor effects against metastasis.
current_roster.name: Assessing a New Immunotherapy for Dogs with Cancer That Has Spread to the Lungs
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine the maximum tolerated dose and efficacy of an immunotherapy protocol against metastatic osteosarcoma or melanoma growing within the lungs. Before your pet begins the study, your pet will need to have the following tests/procedures performed to find out if he/she can be in the study: physical exam, blood tests (including a complete blood count and serum chemistry panel), urinalysis, chest x-rays. If the type of cancer is unknown, additional tests maybe required in order to confirm the type of cancer before being allowed to take part in the study. Lastly, you will undergo training for nebulization of your pet. After this training, you will be sent home with a nebulizer, equipment, and training materials to see if you and your dog are comfortable with twice daily nebulization. Only after determining whether nebulization works for you and your dog will your dog be eligible. If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your pet can take part in the study, the following will happen as part of the study: Your pet will undergo a blood draw to collect up to 4 teaspoons of blood (20 milliliters) and have an ultrasound guided fine needle aspirate of a lung mass performed under sedation as well as baseline chest x-rays. After this, your pet will be discharged and will return to start inhalation therapy in 3 days. The first day of treatments will be performed here at UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital in order to monitor patient compliance, monitor for any complications, and ensure that you are trained and comfortable administering the treatments at home. The remaining 13 days of treatments will be performed by you at home (2 treatments per day). Your pet will receive therapy with inhaled IL-15 twice daily for 14 days. Your dog will return once weekly for one month to receive routine physical examinations and blood tests to ensure that they are tolerating the therapy well. On day17, (the day after completing the treatments), your pet will also undergo another fine needle aspirate of a lung mass. On day 31 (two weeks after completion of treatments), we will also repeat chest x-rays. Chest x-rays will again be taken on day 45, day 73, and day 101 which will conclude the study. If your pets disease progresses and you elect euthanasia, or if your pet dies, we will ask permission to perform a necropsy to obtain samples of the tumors within the lungs.
current_roster.name: Evaluating a new immunotherapy for advanced stage osteosarcoma and melanoma in dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: This is a multi-site study taking place at the University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center, Purdue University, and University of Pennsylvania. We have shown that a drug commonly used to treat heart disease, propranolol, can kill hemangiosarcoma cells in the laboratory. The drug has also been effective in reducing disease progression and increasing the survival time in people with angiosarcoma, a cancer very similar to canine hemangiosarcoma. This study will test three dose levels of propranolol along with standard doxorubicin chemotherapy for safety and benefit to dogs with hemangiosarcoma. Screening to establish eligibility, includes chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiogram, blood and urine tests (X-ray, ultrasound may have been performed prior to screening) Day 1 exam, blood pressure, blood sample, start on oral propranolol tablets During days 4-9, study staff will work with owners and statistician to determine if the dog can move up to the next dose of propranolol PK sampling post-propranolol on Day 11 (small amounts of blood taken over a 24 hour period) Doxorubicin chemotherapy begins on Day 12 with PK sampling post-chemotherapy Rechecks and follow up at every chemotherapy visit (Days 33, 54, 75, 96) plus at 6, 9 and 12 months
current_roster.name: PRO-DOX: Clinical evaluation of propranolol in combination with doxorubicin for the treatment of hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of optical coherence tomography (a non invasive optical imaging technique) for detection of incomplete surgical margins following surgery for skin and subcutaneous tumors in dogs. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: Undergo surgical removal of a skin or subcutaneous tumor at The Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center. Exclusion criteria are suspected lipoma. What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Following surgical excision the tumor specimen will be imaged with optical coherence tomography to assess for residual tumor cells. Following imaging the tumor will be submitted for pathologic assessment. Client Compensation The study will provide an account credit of $100 to help cover the costs of histopathology.
current_roster.name: Using enhanced imaging for residual tumor detection following surgery for skin tumors in dogs

current_roster.description: We are recruiting dogs with osteosarcoma (OSA) of the legs to assess the effectiveness an investigational immunotherapy (STING agonist). A Positron Emission Tomograph - Computed Tomography (PET-CT) scan will be obtained to assess the presence of metastatic disease, i.e., spread of bone cancer beyond the primary tumor, prior to enrollment. All dogs will receive treatment prior to amputation. Two doses of STING agonist immunotherapy separated by 1-2 weeks will be performed under image-guidance directly into the primary bone cancer tumor. All treatments will be performed under general anesthesia or sedation. Within 24-48 hours after the first STING agonist treatment, carboplatin chemotherapy will be given in a vein. At three weeks following immunotherapy, dogs must undergo amputation (or limb sparing surgical excision) followed by an additional 3-5 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy. Serial CT or PET-CT imaging and blood sampling will be performed at 3 month intervals for a year to assess the spread of disease.
current_roster.tagline: Canine Bone Cancer immunotherapy
current_roster.name: Canine Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial

current_roster.description: Intestinal dysbiosis is an alteration in the composition and/or richness of the intestinal microbiota. Intestinal dysbiosis has been associated with tumor progression of colorectal, lung, and breast cancer in human patients. Proposed mechanisms of the microbiomes influence on cancer progression includes direct DNA breakage from bacterial toxins, modulation of the host's cellular survival mechanisms, generation of oxidative stress, and promotion of inflammation and immune dysregulation. The objective of this study is to determine whether or not canine patients diagnosed with osteosarcoma have intestinal dysbiosis and if the presence of intestinal dysbiosis is associated with metastasis in these patients. Due to their similar biological behavior, yet higher incidence rate and shorter lifespan, dogs are an excellent model for spontaneous osteosarcoma in the human. Understanding the role that dysbiosis plays in tumor presentation and metastasis in dogs may give us insight into its association in humans with osteosarcoma. To date, no studies have been published investigating the intestinal microbiota in dogs or humans with osteosarcoma. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.tagline: Dysbiosis in Canine Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Evaluating the association between an altered intestinal microbiome and the development/metastasis of osteosarcoma in dogs

current_roster.description: Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in dogs. Current treatment options include various types of chemotherapy, including TANOVEA-CA1 (rabacfosadine for injection), the first FDA conditionally approved drug to treat canine lymphoma. It is an intravenous chemotherapy agent that has been used both in normal dogs and in more than 600 dogs with cancer. The goal of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the addition of rabacfosadine to a chemotherapy protocol containing doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide and prednisone (CHOP) in dogs with previously untreated, spontaneous, multicentric lymphoma. We hypothesize that dogs that receive this therapy could have outcomes that are better than dogs that receive conventional CHOP treatment without rabacfosadine. Initially pets will undergo a series of diagnostic tests, which will include blood tests, urinalysis, cytology, and chest X-rays. The results of these initial tests will determine if the dog is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are part of the routine testing done in patients with lymphoma. Dogs will receive four infusions each of rabacfosadine, doxorubicin, and vincristine scheduled at specific intervals over an 18-week period. During this time, owners will also be administering oral chemotherapy drugs (cyclophosphamide and prednisone). Weekly visits (except week 14) will be required for lab work and/or chemotherapy administration. Four of those visits may be conducted by the regular veterinarian as they will be for lab work only. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive rabacfosadine, doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone. This study is available at multiple locations (CO, OR, AZ, NC, WI). If you are interested in having your pet participate in this study, please contact the hospital where you wish you participate directly.
current_roster.name: Study to Evaluate the Safety and Efficacy of Rabacfosadine, Vincristine, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin and Prednisone in Dogs with

current_roster.description: NC State University College of Veterinary Medicine is enrolling in a clinical trial investigating the use of a novel radiation-enhancing drug in client owned dogs with osteosarcoma. This is a placebo controlled study, not all dogs will receive the drug but all dogs will receive radiation therapy. Patients will be required to come to NCSU for treatment. Owners must be compliant with study visits, and be willing to complete questionnaires. In addition to routine diagnostics, dogs will participate in non-invasive gait analysis and sensory tests.
current_roster.name: A pilot study to evaluate DNA damage response inhibiting drugs in pet dogs with osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: This randomized, prospective, controlled clinical trial is designed to obtain data to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of Autologous Prescription Product, Code 95A7.50 (unlicensed), also referred to as the ELIAS Cancer Immunotherapy (ECI) as a treatment for dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma. All dogs will undergo amputation of the affected limb and the tumor will be submitted to ELIAS. Dogs will be randomized into one of two cohorts: one cohort will receive the experimental immunotherapy, while the other cohort will receive standard of care chemotherapy, consisting of four (4) doses of carboplatin. The outcomes of the two cohorts will be compared for effectiveness and any adverse events occurring during the study will be noted and assessed.
current_roster.name: Clinical trial to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of surgery combined with ELIAS Cancer Immunotherapy as treatment for appen

current_roster.description: Small cell GI lymphoma is commonly diagnosed in older cats and recommended treatment of this cancer is an oral chemotherapy drug called chlorambucil in combination with prednisolone or prednisone. Despite the wide use of chlorambucil in cats, the pharmacokinetic parameters, i.e. how the body absorbs, metabolizes and eliminates the drug, have not been previously studied in cats. Knowledge of the pharmacokinetic parameters of chlorambucil in this population of older, cancer-bearing cats is critical to understand why some cats experience side effects with chlorambucil therapy and determine if variability in the metabolism of chlorambucil contributes to treatment failure. The purpose of this study is to understand how a cats body absorbs and metabolizes chlorambucil, a commonly used oral cancer drug for cats. There will be about 24 cats taking part in this study. Within 14 days of starting the study treatment, your cat will have a complete blood count, chemistry profile, B12 level, and urinalysis. If determined to be eligible for the study, your cat will return for the first study visit. Your cat will be fasted (no food, water OK) after midnight the day before his/her first study visit (Day 0). On Day 0, your cat will have a baseline blood sample obtained, be administered his/her first dose of chlorambucil and then have three more blood samples collected throughout the day. Each blood sample will be about teaspoon in volume (2 teaspoons total during the day). All cats will be assigned to a specific study group, which will determine the timing of these blood collections. If assigned to Group D, which has a 12-hour post-treatment blood sample collection, you have the option to pick your cat up in the evening or have him/her spend the night at the CSU VTH to go home the following morning. Owners will continue to administer the oral chlorambucil at home once every other day, as is standard for treatment of small cell (low grade) lymphoma in cats. Cats will return on Day 14 for a recheck examination, complete blood count, and collection of another blood sample. Total blood collected from your cat at this visit will be about 1 teaspoon. After this visit, clinical trial participation will be complete.
current_roster.name: Pharmacokinetics of Oral Chlorambucil in Cats with Cancer

current_roster.description: Purpose: Optical coherence imaging (OCT) is a type of optical imaging that can evaluate tissues with microscopic detail without damaging them. The purpose of this study is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of the use of polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) to detect residual tumor following resection of gastrointestinal, skin or subcutaneous tumors in dogs. This clinical investigation will be the first evaluation of PS-OCT imaging in a clinically relevant and heterogenous population of dogs with gastrointestinal, skin and subcutaneous tumors. This investigation aims to improve the accuracy of the surgical margin assessment in companion animals and improve the accuracy of surgical treatment of canine cancer. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must: Cytology or histopathology confirmation of relevant tumor type (except lipoma) Dog undergoing surgical excision of relevant tumor type at OSU What does enrolling in this clinical trial involve? Dogs will undergo surgery to remove their tumor, following removal the tumor will be scanned with polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment. Client Compensation Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive $70 credit to their account to help with the costs of the histopathology evaluation. Contact: Dr. Laura Selmic selmic.1@osu.edu
current_roster.name: Enhanced imaging for surgical margins of skin and gastrointestinal tumors in dogs

current_roster.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in dogs. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.



This study will focus on assessing whether PS-OCT (a new type of optical coherence tomography) could help us improve the accuracy to detect residual cancer in dogs following mammary cancer removal. This project will open the door to veterinarians having the technology to allow accurate real-time interpretation of surgical margins to minimize the necessity for additional surgeries or other treatments and decrease the tumor recurrence.
current_roster.tagline: Detection of remaining cancer after tumor removal
current_roster.name: Detection of remaining cancer cells after removal (Mammary tumors)

current_roster.description: This is a proof of concept study to evaluate preliminary evidence of improved pain and safety of metabolomics-based therapy in dogs with measurable appendicular osteosarcoma (OSA). Osteosarcoma is a common primary bone tumor particularly in medium to giant breed dogs affecting appendicular bones such as the distal radius, proximal humerus, distal femur and proximal tibia. The osteolytic/osteoproductive behavior of this tumor results in significant discomfort. Amputation +/- adjuvant chemotherapy represents the standard treatment approach though amputation may not be ideal due to co-morbidities such as osteoarthritis in other limbs. When amputation is not pursued, hypofractionated radiation therapy +/-bisphosphonate therapy may be used to help manage pain. The Sponsor has generated a therapeutic cocktail which includes bestatin, amethylparatyrosine, dihydrotestosterone and melanotan diluted with 0.9% NaCL delivered as 3 times weekly subcutaneous (SQ) administration. The combination of these agents is proposed to alter tumor cell metabolism and thereby improve pain in dogs with appendicular OSA. This combination of compounds is currently under evaluation in human oncology.
current_roster.name: A FUNDED CLINICAL STUDY FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PAIN IN DOGS WITH OSTEOSARCOMA

current_roster.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.
current_roster.tagline: Ethos-PUSH: Hemangiosarcoma
current_roster.name: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)

current_roster.description: Mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common malignant skin tumor in the dog. While surgery is the main treatment for most MCT, a subset have a high potential for eventual recurrence and spread, and require medical treatment in addition to surgery in an attempt to delay or prevent eventual recurrence. Furthermore, many dogs may present with disease that cannot be removed owing to size, location, or tumors that have already spread. Medical therapy for these patients needs improvement. Both low dose continuous (metronomic) chlorambucil (MC) and toceranib (TOC) have been used safely in dogs with MCT, and the combination is sometimes used in patients. However, the combination has not been scientifically tested for effectiveness. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of this combination given to dogs with measurable MCT. Dogs will receive MC orally once daily, and will receive TOC orally every other day. They will be rechecked 2, 4, 6 and 8 weeks after starting then every 6 weeks thereafter. Visits will generally take about 1 hour. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and the dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease stabilization or meaningful tumor shrinkage). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, CT). Standard bloodwork, urinalysis and blood pressure measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the effect of MC and TOC on immune function. Dogs must come to CSU for all visits related to the study.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Combined Chlorambucil and Toceranib for Treatment of Canine Mast Cell Tumors

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to compare the effectiveness and side effects of two standard-of-care chemotherapy protocols (CHOP vs. LOPP) to see if one is more beneficial for the treatment of T-cell Lymphoma in dogs. Dogs that are enrolled will be randomly assigned to receive either CHOP or LOPP. Participating dogs will have an initial screening visit to assess overall health and confirm eligibility, including a free in-house flow cytometry screen to differentiate between T-cell and B-cell lymphoma. Once eligible for enrollment, the cost of some additional testing is covered and there are gift card incentives at milestone timepoints during the trial. The cost of chemotherapy is not covered and is the responsibility of the pet owner.
current_roster.name: Comparison of the efficacy & impact on suppressor cells of CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy in canine T-cell lymphoma

current_roster.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure. current_roster.name: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial

current_roster.description: Previous studies have demonstrated durable responses to inhaled IL-15 in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma without any recognized toxicity. Unfortunately, IL-15 did not work for the majority of dogs and this may be due to the fact that resident NK cells may not be present or may be exhausted. We are therefore investigating whether the addition of autologous activated NK cells might improve response rates in canine patients receiving inhaled IL-15. The primary endpoints of this study are to determine the safety and preliminary evidence of efficacy for this combination treatment.
current_roster.name: Inhaled IL-15 and Autologous NK Immunotherapy for Treatment of Lung Metastases
current_roster.top_investigator: Robert Rebhun, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety, ideal dose, and effectiveness of a new therapy for oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in cats. Oral SCC is an aggressive cancer that invades locally into bone and soft tissues of the mouth. In cats, the tumors are usually too large to be safely removed with surgery and other treatments are not very effective. STAT3 is a signaling molecule known to function abnormally in many SCC tumors in cats and people and we believe that the STAT3 decoy we are studying may be able to shut off STAT3 function and slow or stop this cancer in cats and people.
current_roster.name: STAT3 Decoy for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: STUDY CLOSED Purpose To evaluate the incidence of tonsillar metastasis based on histopathology in dogs with various types of malignant oral tumors. Background Squamous cell carcinomas and melanomas are common types of oral tumors in dogs. While canine oral squamous cell carcinomas and oral melanomas both are known to metastasize to the tonsil, the incidence of tonsillar metastasis has not been reported in veterinary medicine yet. We do know that primary tonsillar tumors such as tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma can (SCC) behave very aggressively and are also a highly metastatic disease. The prognosis for canine tonsillar SCC is poor, and tonsil tumors, whether primary or metastatic from an oral tumor, generally behave very aggressively. Therefore, an assessment of tonsillar metastasis in dogs with oral tumors will be an important factor for determining the overall prognosis. Study Design Dogs undergoing complete staging of a malignant primary oral tumor at theAnimal Cancer Care and Research Center in Roanoke, VAwill be evaluated for this study. Staging examination: The minimum diagnostics of complete blood count, serum biochemical analysis, fine needle aspiration of bilateral mandibular lymph node, three-view thoracic radiographs, and computed tomography (CT) of the head /neck, thorax and abdomen are required to be included in this study. These are the standard staging procedures for dogs with oral cancer, and are not part of the research study. Bilateral tonsillar and primary oral tumor biopsy: Under general anesthesia, we will perform a thorough oropharyngeal examination, tonsillar assessment, and right and left tonsillar and primary oral tumor biopsies. The biopsy tissues will be submitted to board-certified pathologists. This biopsy will be done specifically for this study. The results of this biopsy will be shared with you, and they may help to guide treatment planning for your dog. Compensation Participants will receive a CT scan, primary tumor and bilateral tonsillar biopsy procedures, histopathology, anesthesia, and oral pain medications at no cost. Owners will be responsible for all other medical fees related to the diagnosis and treatment of their dogs cancer.
current_roster.name: Assessment of Tonsillar Metastasis as Standard Staging Examination in Dogs with Primary Oral Tumors

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to develop a new diagnostic procedure to measure how much oxygen is present in tumors, and how much it is reduced by giving different doses of an oxygen carrying drug (OMX). One of the reasons that tumor cells can be resistant to radiation therapy is that the center of tumors often do not have a lot of oxygen present. This imaging trial is to find the best way of detecting hypoxia with imaging studies, and testing how much we can improve oxygen in the tumor with OMX. We will use this information in future studies to improve response to radiation therapy. There will be about 24 pets taking part in this study.
current_roster.name: Non-invasive measurement of improving oxygen in dog tumors with PET imaging and an oxygen carrying molecule

current_roster.description: GSTs (glutathione-S-transferases)are enzymes which help the body eliminate (detoxify) environmental chemicals and certaindrugs. People that have low activity genetic variants in GSTs have a higher risk of certain cancers, such as lymphoma and bladder cancer, especially if they are exposed to certain chemicals in the environment.We want to determine whether the same is true for dogs. Human patients with low activity GST variants also havea higher risk of toxicities from certain drugsused to treat cancer and immune-mediated diseases. We also want todetermine if this is true in dogs. We are focusing on four canine GST genes, GSTT1, GSTT5 (unique to dogs), GSTM1 and GSTP1. We have found variants that are likely to affect enzyme function in each of these genes in dogs.Our overall goal is to see whether these variants are a risk factor for environmental cancers such as lymphoma, bladder cancer, and other tumorsin dogs, and whether risk for these tumors is a combination of GST variants andexposure to environmental chemicals (as measured in the urine or blood).
current_roster.name: Urinary biomarkers of environmental exposures in dogs with bladder cancer

current_roster.description: Radiation therapy uses high-energy radiation to shrink tumors and kill cancer cells. The radiation is intended to damage the DNA of the cancer cells beyond repair so that they stop dividing or die. Radioembolization with Y90 is an advanced form of radiation therapy that delivers high-dose radiation with precision, enabling precise targeting of a tumor with minimal damage to nearby healthy tissue.Y90 has been used to successfully treat liver tumors in over 100,000 human patients. Studies have revealed that Y90 is well-tolerated by the patient, results in minimal complications or side effects, maintains or improves the quality of life, and results in equivalent survival times when compared to surgery for patients with operable tumors.Eye90 microspheres are currently being studied in humans with liver tumors.
current_roster.name: FIDO TREATS

current_roster.description: The primary purpose of this study will be to assess the safety and effects of Lattice SBRT in the treatment of dogs and cats with very large tumors. This study also seeks to better understand the underlying changes to the tumor itself, as well as the immune system.
current_roster.name: Lattice SBRT for palliation of large tumors

current_roster.description: Many sarcomas in both people and dogs can be resistant to the available treatment options. A new way of fighting these sarcomas is with immunotherapy, which helps the bodys own immune system fight the cancer. There is a type of immune cell in the body, called a macrophage, that normally helps fight bacteria and viruses, as well as helps heal wounds. However, it is also known that macrophages can help sarcomas grow and spread. There is a new drug, a small molecule called NCGC00413972 (NIH 972), which can re-program these macrophages to instead fight against the tumor. This has been shown to be successful in cells and in mice. There is also information that this drug is safe to give to healthy dogs. The primary goal of this trial is to evaluate the safety and biologic effects of NIH 972 in dogs with cancer. A secondary goal of this trial is to evaluate any anti-tumor effects it may have in dogs with sarcomas. If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your dog can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study: On the first day your dog receives the new drug, they will have blood drawn at multiple time points and will be in hospital for close monitoring for at least 8 hours after their first dose. They will either need to stay overnight with us or come back for an additional blood draw 24 hours from their first dose. They will receive a tablet daily and be rechecked 1, 2, 4, and 6 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening, and the drug is well tolerated. On these follow-up visits, we will collect additional blood, both to assess how they are handling the drug and to store for research purposes. If needed to monitor their cancer, they will also have imaging performed at certain visits. Two weeks after starting the drug, they will have another biopsy of their tumor in addition to additional blood draws. Sedation will be required for the biopsies and imaging (if applicable to your dog). In the unfortunate event of your dog passing away or being humanely euthanized while in this trial, a necropsy will be performed to help understand the cause of death.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Treatment for Dogs with Sarcomas
current_roster.name: Phase I Clinical Trial of NCGC00413972 (NIH 972) in Dogs with Spontaneously Occurring Sarcomas

current_roster.description: Randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to assess a potential new treatment for oral melanoma in dogs. Investigational product or placebo will be administered once every 2 weeks for approximately 6 months (15 scheduled visits). All trial visits must occur at one of the designated clinical trial sites. Period lab work and thoracic radiographs will be performed to asses each dog's overall health. Owners are required to sign a consent form before their dog is enrolled, complete owner diaries at home, and complete a single Quality of Life assessment question at each visit.
current_roster.tagline: Dogs with Oral Melanoma
current_roster.name: Oral Melanoma Study in Dogs

current_roster.description: Purpose To evaluate the activity of a type of communication signal released from cells in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas after they are treated with non-invasive histotripsy ablation Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of skin cancer in dogs. They tend to develop slowly and dont usually metastasize when they are low grade. A biopsy is needed to determine the tumor grade. Surgery is the treatment of choice, but if a minimal surgery (removal of only the tumor that can be seen or felt) is performed, the tumor is likely to grow back. Removal of the tumor and several centimeters of normal-appearing tissue is required for complete removal. However, this can be impossible without amputation or the addition of radiation therapy, particularly when the tumors are large or affect certain areas of the body like the limbs or face. Alternative treatments to surgery or radiation are needed. We have previously evaluated a non-surgical, non-radiation, non-thermal focused ultrasound treatment (histotripsy) to kill soft tissue sarcomas affecting pet dogs. This technology has also been used in humans with liver tumors. Histotripsy focuses microsecond-long soundwaves through the skin onto a precise target area of the tumor. This causes air bubbles in the tumor tissue to expand and collapse, mechanically disintegrating the surrounding tumor tissue. Research in rodents, pet dogs, and humans have shown that the liquified tissue stimulates the immune system to recognize cancer in other parts of the body. The purpose of this study is to evaluate one type of communication signal released from cells, termed extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs carry protein and genetic messages that cause immediate changes in the receiving cell. EVs and their cargo can be used as a non-invasive way to diagnose a tumor or look for signals to predict response to treatment or prognosis. We will extract and measure EVs and their immune signal cargo from the liquified tumor tissue, the lymph nodes, and the blood after histotripsy treatment of soft tissue sarcomas. We hope to find that histotripsy increases the number and type of EVs in the blood, which would be the first step in developing a liquid biopsy for diagnosis; we also hope to find that histotripsy treatment changes the communication with the immune system, serving as a mechanism to explain the changes seen in the immune response after histotripsy. To determine how histotripsy may affect EVs, we are recruiting dogs with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo histotripsy treatment of the tumor. An existing tumor must be present for treatment. The application of this experimental therapy has the potential to directly enhance the quality of life of dogs diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas and defray the cost of treatment. At the same time, the results of our study may lead to improved liquid biopsy and treatment options for human cancer patients.
current_roster.tagline: Ultrasound ablation of soft tissue sarcomas
current_roster.name: Treating soft tissue sarcomas in dogs with non-surgical ultrasound ablation

current_roster.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks for 6 vaccines. If no metastases are found at the last staging visit (1 month after the last vaccine), dogs will then receive 6 monthly boosters for life or until progression. Alternatively, if early metastases (single or multiple small lung nodules " 700 dogs with melanoma or OSA) will be treated and monitored for an hour, with resolutions of symptoms the dog will be returned to the owner. In future vaccinations, these dogs will receive an antihistamine medication 20 min prior to vaccination. In the unlikely event that the vaccine sites/dog show severe changes such as pain, inflammation, necrosis with ulceration, dermatitis, or severe swelling the dog will be treated.
current_roster.name: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: Cutaneous epitheliotropic lymphoma is a rare neoplastic condition in dogs. Current treatment options are limited and duration of response is often short. Laverdia-CA1 (verdinexor) is a conditionally approved oral tablet for treatment of lymphoma in dogs. Laverdia has been evaluated for the treatment of multicentric nodal lymphoma but has not yet been evaluated for the treatment of cutaneous epitheliotropic lymphoma.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of Laverdia-CA1 (verdinexor) for Treatment of Naïve Canine Cutaneous Epitheliotropic Lymphoma

current_roster.description: Verdinexor is a chemotherapy drug that has been conditionally approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine lymphoma. Verdinexor is a selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE) compound, and this family of drug has demonstrated encouraging results in preclinical studies when combined with other chemotherapeutic drugs. These studies offer encouragement that these types of combinations and clinical results could be achieved in dogs. This study seeks to establish the tolerability of verdinexor in combination with doxorubicin in dogs with cancer. The results of this study could be used to advance the study of this combination of drugs in future clinical trials that focus on a specific cancer types. The study duration is 120 days and consists of a total of 10 hospital visits. The trial is fully funded with no costs to the owner.
