current_roster.description: A large number of different canine and human cancers appear to rely on signaling through 2 important cellular pathways; the MAPK pathway and the PI3K/mTOR pathway. The drugs trametinib and sapanisertib, which target signaling through these 2 pathways, appear to have significant antitumor effects both in tissue culture and in mouse models. When these 2 drugs were given to laboratory dogs at the doses we plan to test, they were well tolerated and the amount of drug appearing in the blood was predicted to be enough to inhibit tumor growth. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety, biologic effects, and antitumor activity of combined trametinib and sapanisertib given to dogs with measurable malignant tumors. Your dog will receive trametinib orally once daily and sapanisertib orally every other day. They will be rechecked 6 days, and 2, 4, and 8 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening and the drugs are well tolerated. Visits will generally take about 1 hour, except for the first visit and the Day 6 and Week 4 visits, which may take several hours or all day. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (disease is stable or smaller). Analysis for tumor response will be performed by direct tumor measurement or through the use of imaging (X-rays, ultrasound). Standard bloodwork and urinalysis measurement will be performed at each visit. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the amount of trametinib and sapanisertib appearing in the blood and for changes in other blood markers. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons. Before starting treatment and after 6 days and 4 weeks, your dog will have a small sample of tumor tissue removed through a biopsy to look for changes in signaling in the tumor cells, if your dog’s tumor is in a location where it can be biopsied. This helps us know if the drugs are finding their targets in the cancer cells. This biopsy will require short acting sedation, and your dog may receive several days of oral pain medication after the procedure.
current_roster.tagline: Novel Therapy for Dogs with Cancer
current_roster.name: Combination Trametinib and Sapanisertib Clinical Trial Pilot Study for Canine Malignant Neoplasia

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine / piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer also known as urothelial carcinoma. We will evaluate tumor response, clinical side effects, and quality of life as part of this study. Additionally, we will evaluate immune response and characterize the stool and urine microbiome and metabolome to understand the potential effects of the probiotic. Our broader goal is to improve cancer care and outcomes in dogs with bladder cancer.
current_roster.name: TCC Probiotic

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, efficacy and anti-cancer immune stimulation of a novel method of delivering radiation therapy, lattice radiation therapy, in cats with measurable oral squamous cell carcinoma. Lattice radiation therapy is special type of stereotactic radiation therapy utilizing a state-of-the-art linear accelerator that has on board advanced imaging capabilities and sophisticated software to deliver precisely-targeted radiation at much higher doses, in only a few treatments, as compared to traditional radiation therapy. This permits maximum dose delivery within the target while minimizing dose to the surrounding healthy tissue to minimize side effects. SBRT is used routinely to treat brain tumors in veterinary medicine and has been used to treat various cancers in cats.
current_roster.name: FOSCC Lattice

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.
current_roster.tagline: feline metastatic mammary carcinoma
current_roster.name: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF A NOVEL ANTI-CANCER THERAPEUTIC FOR THE TREATMENT OF METASTATIC MAMMARY CARCINOMA IN CATS

visible_sc_items.label: Genetic (gene transfer, stem cell, recombinant DNA

current_roster.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection. One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general.

current_roster.description: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common oral tumor in cats and this cancer shares many similarities with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck of people. This tumor is very aggressive in both cats and people and new treatments are greatly needed. This study is investigating a novel oral drug, called a lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD-1) inhibitor, that has been shown to slow the growth and metastasis of oral squamous cell carcinoma in people and mice in laboratory models. This medication has not been previously used in the treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma in cats and the goals of this study are to establish the dosing, safety and anti-cancer properties when given to cats that have been diagnosed with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Cats participating in this study will have a low dose of the study medication administered in the hospital followed by collection of small amounts of blood throughout the day. These blood samples will be submitted to a lab to determine what dose of medication your cat will receive as part of this study. Once your cats dose of the study drug has been determined (approximately one week after the 1st study visit), your cat will return for tumor biopsies under either heavy sedation or general anesthesia. Some cats will also have a PET/CT scan performed at this visit. You will be dispensed the study medication to give at home once daily for the next three weeks. You cat will have weekly study visits for the next three weeks for examinations and blood collection to make sure they are tolerating the study medication. At the final study visit, your cat will be sedated or anesthetized for additional tumor biopsies +/- a PET/CT scan, if one was performed at the beginning of the clinical trial.

current_roster.description:
Canine histiocytic sarcoma (HS) is a highly aggressive and often fatal type of cancer that occurs more frequently in certain breeds, including Bernese mountain dog (BMD) (>25%), flat-coated retriever (36%), golden retriever, Rottweiler, and miniature schnauzer. Dogs with HS invariably carry a poor prognosis due to a rapid disease progression and limited effective clinical arsenal.

First line conventional chemotherapy, Lomustine, provides a response rate of 29% for only a median of 96 days

In this proposed trial, we will investigate a novel drug, Trametinib, to determine the antitumor activity (shrinkage of tumor) of the drug in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma using progression-free survival (PFS).

PFS is defined as the percentage of dogs that are progression-free at 6-months post treatment initiation.

Clinical Protocol: - Prior to treatment, a tumor biopsy, and a blood sample (less than one ounce) will be collected. - Upon enrollment, every patient will undergo a complete history, physical examination, laboratory analysis, blood pressure measurement, and diagnostic imaging. - Trametinib will be administered orally, once daily, indefinitely as long as progressive disease is not observed (i.e., stable, partial, or complete response). - The dog will need to return for evaluation of tumor response and/or monitoring of side effects at week 2, then every 4 weeks until week 14, and then every 8 weeks thereafter, until there is evidence of disease progression. - The dog will return for evaluation (physical examination, clinical laboratory assessment of blood, and tumor measurements) on week 2. - Starting on week 4, and every other 4 weeks until week 14, blood and urine sample will be taken, and x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be repeated to monitor your dog’s response to treatment. - Cardiology consultations (Paid by owner)during Pre-treatment, week 6, week 14 and every 8 weeks till progressive disease. - Starting on week 14, the rechecks will be spaced out to every 8 weeks.

Adverse Events (AEs) will also be evaluated at any unscheduled visit. Owners will be asked to fill out Quality of Life questionnaires prior to study.

current_roster.description:
Melanoma is the most dangerous form of skin cancer and kills over 9,300 people a year in the US. Melanoma is also the most common oral cancer in companion dogs and like human melanoma, it is an aggressive cancer that spreads to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, brain, and kidney.

Unfortunately, once melanoma spreads to distant sites, it is usually incurable. Despite advances in standard-of-care therapies (e.g., surgery, radiation therapy (RT) , and chemotherapy), the average survival in dogs with melanoma of advanced stage is less than one year after diagnosis, and less than 6 months if the melanoma has already spread. Therefore, as in human melanoma, new treatments for canine melanoma are needed to improve survival. Treatments that activate the patient's own immune system (immunotherapy) to fight the melanoma have worked very well in some human and dog patients.

We are evaluating a combination of 3 types of therapy all of which have shown immune activation and anti-melanoma activity as single therapies in patients with melanoma. The three therapies include: administration of an immune stimulant directly into the tumor, radiation therapy targeted at the primary tumor, and intravenous administration of an antibody that potentially enhances the body's immune response to the melanoma. We hypothesize that by combining these therapies, we will be able to further extend the life of patients with melanoma.

There are 3 parts to this study: Part 1 has been completed, and we have determined the dose of the immune stimulant to be administered directly into the tumor; In Part 2, the immune stimulant was combined with radiation therapy targeted at the same tumor, and; in Part 3 (Aim 1), the immune stimulant was administered to all sites of palpable disease in addition to the treatments in Part 2. Both Part 2 and Part 3 (Aim 1) are completed.

In Part 3 the immune stimulant is administered directly into the tumor combined with intravenous (IV) Anti-PD1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor , [ICI]) and radiation therapy directed at the primary oral tumor. The information from this study will guide further clinical trials in both dogs and humans.

Owner Responsibility The owner is expected to make and keep all appointments according to the study protocol. The pet will receive the first ICI therapy and then will receive the RT treatment 2 weeks later along with the second ICI treatment. Six days after the RT treatment, your dog’s tumor will be injected with the IT-IC treatment for 3 consecutive days. ICI treatments will be given 3 more times at 3-week intervals. Chest X-rays will be performed prior to treatment and every 6 weeks thereafter. A biopsy of the tumor and blood/urine sample collection will be performed prior to treatment, on the day they receive RT, on the day they receive the first IT-IC, and again 2 and 5 weeks later.

DNA methylation (transformation of normal cells to cancer cells at DNA level) is a critically important modification in cancer cells, which use this mechanism to activate cancer genes and silence of tumor-suppressor genes. Targeting DNA methylation in cancer using DNA hypomethylating drugs reprograms tumor cells to a more normal-like state by affecting multiple pathways, and also sensitizes these cells to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of two DNA hypomethlating drugs TdCyd and Aza-TdC when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. - A biopsy will be collected prior to the first dose of drug (pre-treatment), on Day 8, Day 12 and possibly on Day 22 depending on how the dog has responded to therapy. - The dog will return to UW Veterinary Care on Days 8, 12, 15 and 22. - Serial blood collections (5 time points) will occur on Day 1 of the study. Subsequent, single time point collections will occur on Days 8, 12, 15 and 22. - You will be required to administer doses of TdCyd or Aza-TdC at home on Days 2, 3, 4 and 5 and on Days 9, 10, 11. Your clinician will provide instructions on when and how to provide this medication to your dog.

If the dog’s cancer responds well to the treatment they have been assigned, you will have the option to continue to give the same treatment to your dog for an additional 22 days. During that time, owner will need to continue to regularly visit UW Veterinary Care for blood collection, as well as a biopsy of the dog’s tumor.

current_roster.description:
Purpose
To evaluate the use of urine samples as a liquid biopsy tool to monitor disease progression in canine osteosarcoma

Background
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs, and it often spreads aggressively. In dogs, metastasis develops in more than 80% of cases. Even with treatment, more than 90% of affected dogs do not survive for more than two years following diagnosis.

Our team has developed a technique (Raman molecular analysis) that can detect changes in the urine that are associated with tumor growth. In this study, we are testing this tool to see how different types of treatment given to dogs with osteosarcoma affect what we’re able to detect in the urine. We’ll use these results to further refine the Raman molecular analysis technique so that it can be more useful in helping us understand and predict the behavior of osteosarcoma.

This study is funded by Virginia Tech’s Focused Ultrasound Innovation Fund.

current_roster.description:
In the field of veterinary oncology, identification of metastatic disease is critical for determining
the extent of disease, prognosis, and for developing treatment plans. For many cancer types,
metastasis occurs via the lymphatic system and the status of the draining lymph nodes is an
important part of the pre- and intraoperative evaluation. The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the
primary lymph node draining the tumour and although one might expect that it is the first lymph
node downstream from the tumour, this is not always true. Failure to identify and assess the
sentinel lymph node can lead to incomplete treatment, worse prognosis and poor patient outcome.
Currently in veterinary patients, there are not good protocols in place to identify sentinel lymph
nodes. The development of these protocols could help us to decrease the number of lymph nodes
we remove, in addition to ensuring we are accurately evaluating the most important lymph node
for making follow-up treatment recommendations.

You will be responsible for bringing your pet to the OVC-HSC for both the CT scan and surgery
(may occur during the same visit). In addition, you are expected to pay for the standard costs for
the preoperative staging, including the CT scan and surgery for removal of the tumour and lymph
nodes. Like any medication, the clinical trial treatment may have a low rate of side effects. This
study does not cover the costs of hospitalization or other costs associated with complications
related or unrelated to the clinical trial.
You are expected to return to the Ontario Veterinary College for follow-up appointments as
outlined by your clinician and the clinical trial protocol.

The commitment to participate in this study is no different than if your pet was undergoing a CT
scan and surgery for their tumour. In this study, we are considering what is already standard of
care (CT and surgery) and trying to improve this process. For the CT scan, in addition to
receiving a contrast agent intravenously, as is always performed for these cases, we will also
inject a similar agent locally. With this injection, we will attempt to identify the lymph node that
first drains the tumour, also known as the sentinel lymph node. This information will be
compared to our findings in surgery and on histopathology when the tissues are submitted.
Following the procedure, your pet will be monitored for several hours to ensure they do not
develop any complications from the injection. Surgery will be planned for within 1 week of the
CT scan and may be as soon as the day following.
Time Commitment
For this study, your pet will present for the CT scan as is routinely arranged by the oncology
service. You do not need to make any changes to your plans or expectations. Your pet will then
return for surgery following routine planning. To be included in the study, your pet must have
surgery within 1 week of the CT scan to ensure that no major changes in the tumour growth have
occurred.

current_roster.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.

current_roster.description:
When patients undergo fractionated radiation therapy, maintaining appetite, consistent stools, and body weight are incredibly important for patient well-being and quality of life. The most common non-radiation complications in dogs undergoing these longer radiation protocols include diarrhea, vomiting or regurgitation, and decreased appetite. When these complications happen in patients, both owners and clinicians attempt to offer a multitude of foods, home cooked diets, probiotics, appetite stimulants, anti-nausea medications, or antibiotics. Recently nutritionists and veterinarians at a well-known pet food manufacturer developed a prescription diet designed to specifically help nourish and support dogs that are fighting cancer. This diet is highly digestible and contains a proprietary blend of prebiotic fibers to help support a healthy gastrointestinal microbiome to provide consistent stool quality. The goal of this study is to evaluate the acceptance of the novel diet through food intake and eating enthusiasm data by dogs undergoing daily, definitive intent radiation therapy, and to examine the differences in body weight changes, muscle condition scoring, body condition scoring, body fat index, quality of life, and stool consistency over time in dogs receiving the novel vs control diet.


If your dog participates in this study, he/she will have blood work, urine panel, fecal analysis, and will be randomized to receive one of the two study foods during radiation therapy. Blood work and fecal analysis will be performed prior to starting radiation therapy, half way through radiation, at the end of the radiation protocol and two weeks after completing radiation. Urine panel will be performed prior to starting radiation, at the final radiation dose, and at the two week recheck. We will assess intake of the diet and enthusiasm of the diet twice weekly. We ask that you also record food intake and eating enthusiasm twice a week, fecal scores at each defecation, and quality of life weekly with provided guides and questionnaires. You and your clinical team will be blinded to which diet your dog is receiving, but this will be revealed at the conclusion of the study period.

current_roster.description: In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of a type of white blood cell known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells that are made from the blood of a healthy donor dog. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. In this study, we will use iNKT cells that express a cancer targeting receptor known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the modified iNKT cells to the cancer cells which are then killed. The CAR-iNKT cells also will further activate the patient's own immune system to help kill the cancer cells. The purpose of this study is to determine the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, their maximum tolerated dose, how long they will remain in the patient and their effectiveness against bone cancer that has spread to the lungs.

current_roster.description:
About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells ("fighter" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This "upgrade" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!


In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome.


Who qualifies


Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor

Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor

Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor


Study activities and Timeline


Visit 1 | Day-17

  1. Exam
  2. Blood draw to create CAR T cells
  3. Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week

Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3

  1. On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection

Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3

  1. The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams

Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10

  1. The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor.

Visit 5 | Month 3

  1. We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response


Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI.
current_roster.tagline: CAR T Cell and verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
current_roster.name: CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs

current_roster.description:
Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.


Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated. In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity). After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication. This is an out-patient procedure.
current_roster.tagline: Nasal Electrochemotherapy
current_roster.name: Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. J. Impellizeri DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), MRCVS, CMO

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of K9-ACV, an autologous killed tumor cell vaccine combined with a novel checkpoint inhibitor (CD200AR-L), compared to standard-of-care chemotherapy for the treatment of canine appendicular osteosarcoma (OSA). K9-ACV has safely been used in over 1,000 dogs and the vaccine has been shown to display safety in a previous study (without the addition of the checkpoint inhibitor). By evaluating K9-ACV, this trial aims to advance safer, immune-based treatment options for canine cancer that may offer comparable or superior outcomes to chemotherapy.


Participating patients will be required to complete standard pre-enrollment screening that involves a physical exam, blood work, chest x-rays, and abdominal ultrasound. If the patient passes the screening, they will undergo limb amputation and be randomly assigned to the K9-ACV group or the carboplatin group. Patients in the K9-ACV group will receive an intradermal injection of the checkpoint inhibitor and then will return to the study site 24 hours later for the vaccine administration. Vaccines will be given every 3 weeks for a total of 3 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial vaccine administration for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays. Patients in the chemotherapy group will be treated every 3 weeks for a total of 4 treatments. Patients will return at 4, 6, and 8 months after initial chemotherapy treatment for a physical exam, blood work, and x-rays.
current_roster.tagline: Autologous Cancer Vaccine with Checkpoint Inhibitor for Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma
current_roster.name: Autologous Cancer Vaccine with Checkpoint Inhibitor for Treatment of Canine Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description:
In this study, we will test a new research medication that combines a chemotherapy drug called MMAE (monomethyl Auristatin E) and a light-sensitive drug (Pc-413) and a laser light source (photodynamic therapy) to kill cancer cells in the prostate and in other areas of the body (metastatic disease). These two agents are linked to a molecule that binds to PSMA (prostate specific membrane antigen), a cell surface marker that is produced by prostatic cancer in large quantities. The research medication is inactive until it binds to PSMA. When the research medication binds to PSMA it is taken into the cell and activated. This means the research medication is targeted specifically to prostate cancer cells. The overall goal is to use this new research medication that is specific to prostate cancer cells to kill the cancer.


This study will cover the specific study related diagnostics once your dog is enrolled:

• Chest X-rays

• Abdominal ultrasound

• Prostate aspirate

• Blood work (CBC and chemistry)

• Urinalysis

• Physical examination


All costs associated with the theranostic infusions and laser will be covered by the study including the fees associated with hospitalization. The study will cover the cost of the recheck visits every 2 months following the treatments, including the physical examination, blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound fees. If your dog needs sedation for any of the study related procedures, the study will cover the cost of the sedation as well.
current_roster.tagline: New Treatment for Canine Prostatic Carcinoma
current_roster.name: PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. David Holt, BVSc, Professor of Surgery, Diplomate (ACVS)

current_roster.description:
No chemotherapies have been FDA-approved for use in cats despite a growing need for such therapies. Paclitaxel (Taxol®) is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer therapy today, with potent activity against a variety of cancers in people that also occur in cats. Paclitaxel has been found to kill cancer cell lines isolated from cat tumors in the laboratory, but only one small study has been published evaluating paclitaxel treatment of cats with cancer. In that study, 5 of 9 patients responded to paclitaxel therapy, with 4 of these patients experiencing stable disease and one patient experiencing a partial response. 


The current FDA-approved formulation of paclitaxel for use in people, which uses a cremophor-based agent to solubilize the drug for injection, causes allergic reactions in dogs and cats. This characteristic of the FDA-approved formulation has largely prevented its use in pets. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal® Vet, uses a formulation that has been created to minimize allergic reactions and therefore improve tolerability. Several clinical trials have been performed or are ongoing with this formulation in dogs, but to date, no studies in cats using Paccal Vet have been undertaken. 


The primary purpose of this study is to test the tolerability of Paccal Vet in cats and to determine an acceptable dose. A secondary, exploratory goal is to see whether Paccal Vet may have anti-tumor activity in various tumors in cats. In this context, “exploratory” means that this study is not large enough to prove whether or not Paccal Vet is working in feline cancer. However, the results could help the drug developer determine whether the drug might have the potential to do so. 


The “investigational” part of the study is to test whether Paccal Vet is safe for use in cats and whether the drug may induce an anti-tumor response against their cancer. Paccal Vet is an investigational drug, which means it has not yet been approved by the FDA for use in dogs or cats. The potential benefits and safety of Paccal Vet in the treatment of cats with various cancer types have not yet been demonstrated. The purpose of this study is to test the investigational use of Paccal Vet rather than to provide medical treatment to your cat.


Cats enrolled in the study will receive Paccal Vet via intravenous infusion over 15-30 minutes once every 3 weeks for up to four doses. Throughout those treatment cycles, cats will be monitored carefully for tumor responses and adverse events through physical examinations, blood work, and quality of life questionnaires.
current_roster.tagline: A dose-finding study of Paccal Vet in cats with spontaneous solid tumors
current_roster.name: A dose-finding study of Paccal Vet in cats with spontaneous solid tumors

current_roster.description:
The aim of this study is to perform initial testing for ablation (tumor killing) of mammary or skin tumors through a new noninvasive technology. An injection of magnetic nanoparticles (FDA approved) into the tumor can help concentrate the heat in the tumor to kill the tumor. Ultimately the idea is that this noninvasive technology could be used as an alternative to surgical removal of the mammary or skin or subcutaneous tumor.


Each dog will receive sedation and an ultrasound-guided injection of the tumor with the magnetic nanoparticles, then, after four hours, will have general anesthesia to have the tumor ablated with the novel system. Following the procedure, the dog will be discharged.


Client Compensation:

The costs of the following will be covered as part of the study: sedation and administration of the magnetic nanoprobe, the magnetic nanoprobe, anesthesia for the ablation, the ablation, a $1461 account credit to cover budgeted anesthesia and surgery costs, and histopathology. In addition, as a study participant, you will be provided with a $500 direct payment to help cover other costs associated with the treatment of the mammary or skin, or subcutaneous tumor.
current_roster.tagline: Use of magnetic nanoprobes for ablation of canine mammary, skin and subcutaneous tumors
current_roster.name: Use of magnetic nanoprobes for ablation of canine mammary, skin and subcutaneous tumors
current_roster.top_investigator: Laura Selmic, MPH, DACVS-SA, DECVS, Surgical Oncology

current_roster.description: This is a randomized two-arm pilot study comparing dogs with advanced melanoma treated with nanoparticle calreticulin based immunotherapy combined with a focused ultrasound (HIFU) with or without an immune checkpoint inhibitor (anti-PDL-1). We have previously demonstrated that delivering a calreticulin (CRT) expression plasmid via a cationic liposome nanoparticle (CRT-NP) generates an immunostimulatory signal in mice tumors, akin to the immunogenic cell death-associated external cell membrane-bound CRT induced by radiation. CRT is a well-known multifunctional chaperone protein involved in cellular calcium homeostasis and immune modulation. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate local and systemic (abscopal) immune effects of CRT-NP based immunotherapy in combination with HIFU with and without an anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor). Dogs will receive CRT-NP intratumorally once weekly for 4-8 weeks along with HIFU applied weekly to the same tumors. An anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody will be administered intravenously every 2 weeks, three days post HIFU treatment. Dogs will undergo baseline comprehensive lab work and urinalysis, which will also be monitored throughout treatment. A baseline CT scan or radiographs will be performed and repeated 12 weeks after the start of treatment to monitor for metastasis/progression of disease. Tumor volume will be measured at each visit along with adverse event reporting at each visit as well according to the VCOG Criteria for Adverse Events v. 2020. Tumor biopsies will be performed to monitor immune modulation, T cell infiltration, myeloid markers, and cytokine response. Dogs with a durable response will be monitored long term every 2-3 months. This study has been approved by the UTSW Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
current_roster.tagline: Immunotherapy and High Frequency Ultrasound in Dogs with Advanced Melanoma
current_roster.name: Nanoparticle CRT Combined with High Frequency Ultrasound with or without Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Dogs with Advanced Melanoma
current_roster.top_investigator: Ashish Ranjan, BVsc, PhD, Vice Chair Research Innovations Comp. Oncology

current_roster.description:
The CHECKMATE-K9 study is a pilot clinical trial at the UW Veterinary Cancer Center, investigating the safety and tolerability of combining two immune checkpoint inhibitors (VGS-001 (anti-CTLA4) and VGS-002 (anti-PD-1)) in dogs with measurable solid tumors. All enrolled dogs will receive this concurrent intravenous therapy every three weeks for four doses over a 9-week treatment period, followed by a 12-week observation period.


The study is open-label and exploratory, focusing primarily on assessing safety and tolerability. Secondary objectives include the overall response rate and biological activity.


The study covers all required examination visits, lab work, diagnostic imaging, and investigational drug costs. It also allocates up to $1500 per patient for adverse event treatment during the 12-week study and covers necropsy costs if a study-related adverse event leads to death or euthanasia. The screening process is not covered by the trial.
current_roster.tagline: Dual immunotherapy (Checkpoint inhibitors) for dogs with cancer
current_roster.name: CHECKMATE-K9

current_roster.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.
current_roster.tagline: Glioma Immunotherapy (Nanomedicine) and radiation
current_roster.name: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy

current_roster.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that present a significant therapeutic challenge in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by their locally invasive behavior and limited overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds, particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers, are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy can be delivered alone also, through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), the latter offering greater precision and tissue sparing and short duration treatments. Despite these interventions, prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. The natural disease progression, intact immune system, and comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable in assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy, particularly the use of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered immune cells. CAR technology involves modifying immune cells to express tumor-targeting receptors, enabling them to recognize and destroy cancer cells with heightened specificity. Notably, CAR-engineered neutrophils have demonstrated the ability to traverse the blood-brain barrier—an essential feature for treating intracranial tumors.

A pivotal safety study of CAR neutrophils in dogs was recently conducted at Purdue University, followed by preclinical efficacy testing in murine models of glioma. These genetically modified cells showed potential in targeting brain tumors with minimal off-target toxicity. Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma. The rationale is to transform the tumor microenvironment through CAR neutrophils, potentially enhancing the efficacy and outcome of radiation therapy. This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.
current_roster.tagline: CAR neutrophils and Radiation  for Dog's glioma
current_roster.name: CAR neutrophils and Radiation to treat glioma in the dog

current_roster.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin or carboplatin and temozolomide with propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin or carboplatin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

current_roster.name: Evaluation of a combination of three drugs in dogs with hemangiosarcoma

current_roster.description:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC.


If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.
current_roster.tagline: New combination treatment for dogs with bladder tumors
current_roster.name: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The goal of the study is to assess the microscopic extension of soft tissue sarcomas. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically or histologically diagnosed soft tissue sarcomas that are undergoing a wide excision. Wide surgical excision, defined as three-centimeter lateral margins and of layer of fascia (dense tissue) deep to the mass, will be performed as the standard of care. While under general anesthesia and immediately prior to routine surgery, sterile tattoo ink will be used to mark specific margins around the tumor. All tattoo ink will be within the tumor sample and planned margin with no tattoo ink applied outside the tissue to be removed.


There are no additional costs associated with the study beyond those acquired through routine care for the underlying condition. The study provides only costs toward the surgical procedure (mass removal) itself and the histopathology (biopsy) charges. This combination of charges would typically be $441-$1074 depending on tumor size. All other costs are the responsibility of the owner.
current_roster.tagline: Soft tissue sarcoma undergoing wide excision
current_roster.name: Characterization of Soft Tissue Sarcoma Microscopic Extension
current_roster.top_investigator: Hunter Piegols, DVM, DACS-SA, ACVS Fellow-Surgical Oncology

current_roster.description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.
current_roster.tagline: Finding Draining Lymph Nodes in Anal Sac Tumors in Dogs
current_roster.name: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery

current_roster.description:
Purpose

To evaluate the effects of histotripsy, a high-precision ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with oral tumors. 


Background

Histotripsy is an emerging technology that uses focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team’s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. Additionally, histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects oral tumors in dogs. 


Study Design

Dogs will undergo CT and/or MRI scans (if not obtained previously during diagnostics) to visualize the oral tumor and plan the histotripsy treatment. The histotripsy treatment approach will be patient-specific to accommodate for unique tumor sizes and locations.  

On the day of treatment, hair will be removed from the area overlying the tumor to allow for maximum transmission of the ultrasound waves. Histotripsy treatment will be delivered non-invasively through the skin to mechanically disintegrate the underlying tumor. Dogs will be maintained and monitored under anesthesia. After the treatment, images (CT and/or MRI) will be taken to assess the immediate effects of the ultrasound treatment. Most patients recover uneventfully and go home the same day.

One day after the completion of histotripsy treatment, dogs will undergo standard-of-care surgical resection. This allows us to assess the effects of the ultrasound treatment. At this point, participation in the study is complete.
current_roster.tagline: Histotripsy to treat oral tumors in dogs
current_roster.name: Non-invasive treatment of oral tumors in dogs

current_roster.description:
Background

Equine sarcoids are the most common skin tumors in horses, associated with bovine papillomavirus (BPV). These locally invasive tumors lead to lesions that cause discomfort, pain, and functional limitations, significantly impacting a horse’s quality of life. Sarcoids are persistent and prone to recurrence, making their removal essential for preventing complications like infections or interference with tack. Current treatments, including surgery and cryotherapy, can be invasive, inconsistent, and have high recurrence rates, emphasizing the need for novel, effective solutions.

Histotripsy is a non-invasive ultrasound therapy that uses focused ultrasound waves to create microbubbles that mechanically disrupt targeted tissue. Unlike thermal methods, histotripsy’s non-thermal mechanism ensures precise ablation with minimal damage to surrounding tissues. Developed for human medicine, histotripsy shows promise in veterinary applications due to its precision, real-time imaging, and adaptability.

Non-invasive therapeutics like histotripsy are vital for improving animal welfare, minimizing recovery time, and reducing risks associated with invasive procedures. For equine sarcoids, histotripsy could offer a safe, precise, and effective alternative that could transform treatment outcomes and set a new standard of care for equine cutaneous neoplasia.
current_roster.tagline: A Non-Invasive Approach to treating Equine Sarcoids
current_roster.name: Histotripsy ultrasound therapy effectiveness on equine sarcoids

current_roster.description:
Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat.


3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach.


Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. Some of these follow-up visits can be done with your regular veterinarian if you choose; however, the study will not be able to cover the costs of these visits.
current_roster.tagline: 3-D Printed Implant to Save Leg in Dogs with Bone Cancer
current_roster.name: 3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor

current_roster.description:
In collaboration with the UW Carbone Cancer Center, we are developing an innovative treatment for canine Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (PTCL). This study aims to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and optimal dosage of ⁹⁰Y-NM600 targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) in dogs with PTCL. Our research indicates that targeted RPT can effectively reach tumors, regardless of tumor location.


Please note that this is not a double-masked trial; ALL enrolled patients will receive the targeted RPT.


This funded study (after initial screening) covers the following expenses:

  1. All required examination visits EXCEPT for the initial screening visit.
  2. All laboratory work (CBC, blood chemistry, urinalysis), EXCLUDING the initial lab work needed for initial screening.
  3. Tumor Biopsy
  4. PET-CT scans.
  5. Hospitalization.
  6. All costs related to RPT.
  7. Additionally, up to $1,000 is available to help manage any treatment-related side effects, should they occur.
  8. Please be aware that there is no financial incentive for enrolling your pet in this trial. 


Dogs showing a positive response or stable disease at the day 21 assessment may be eligible for an additional 90Y-NM600 dose.


Dogs with progressive disease will be withdrawn from the study and offered either standard of care chemotherapy (at the clients expense) or treatment discontinuation, based on the client's preference.


Please note that the standard of care chemotherapy is NOT part of the trial.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new targeted radiation therapy for dogs with Peripheral  T-cell lymphoma
current_roster.name: Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (RPT) in Companion Dogs with Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL)
current_roster.top_investigator: David Michael Vail, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), Professor

current_roster.description:
Dogs can develop a serious blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This disease often gets worse quickly, and there is no standard treatment that reliably helps dogs live longer.

This study is testing a drug called trametinib to see if it may help dogs with AML. Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study.


Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done:

• A physical exam by a veterinarian

• Blood tests to check blood counts and organ health

• Urine tests

• A cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response

• Regular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 weeks through Week 12, and approximately every 4 weeks thereafter while dogs remains on study

• Dogs will take trametinib by mouth once daily at home

• Dogs will also take prednisone as directed by your veterinarian
current_roster.tagline: Trametinib clinical trial in dogs with AML
current_roster.name: Clinical Trial of Trametinib in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

current_roster.description:
Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. Standard treatment is amputation and chemotherapy with median survival around 13 months. Some patients are not candidates for amputation due to obesity, orthopedic conditions or other mitigating circumstances. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.
current_roster.tagline: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Electrochemotherapy of Bone with Cementoplasty
current_roster.name: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation

current_roster.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.
current_roster.tagline: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
current_roster.name: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
current_roster.top_investigator: Dr. Geoffrey Wood, DVM, PhD, DVSc Geoffrey Wood

current_roster.description:
Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.
current_roster.tagline: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
current_roster.name: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery

current_roster.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.


What happens in this study

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesia


  1. Minimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatment


  1. Intravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeks


  1. Concurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)


  1. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time points


  1. Overnight hospitalization following biopsy procedures


  1. Follow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-ins


  1. Completion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effects


  1. End of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.
